Even though “Protestantism” appears in the dataset as a “Scale” type variable, we can move it to the “Factors” box and it will automatically be treated as a “Nominal” categorical variable; a small black star next to the variable type icon will signal that the variable was “forced” into behaving like a “Factor”:







When done, you should be seeing some of these outputs:






Questions

What is the expected Social_trust level of a country that does not have a dominant Protestant population?
What is the expected Social_trust level of a country that has a dominant Protestant population?
How much higher or lower is the expected Social_trust in a Protestant country compared to a non-protestant one?








TipSolution






Non-Protestant: the intercept, 24.81% (the mean of the 51 non-Protestant countries).
Protestant: 24.81 + 23.45 = 48.26% (the mean of the 9 Protestant countries).
Difference: 23.45 percentage points higher in Protestant countries. With a single binary predictor, the regression coefficient is simply the difference between the two group means. R² = 0.357: the Protestant/non-Protestant distinction alone accounts for about 36% of the cross-national variation in trust.




The interpretation of the coefficients is exactly the same as in the previous case (Regions), with the exception that now we only have one category to compare against the “reference” because the Protestantism variable is naturally dichotomous/binary one, containing only two categories.
Because of this, we could treat Protestantism as a “Scale” type variable and enter it into the “Covariates” box instead, and still get the same coefficients because it would be treated as a theoretically infinite scale on which we only observe two data points in practice (0 as non-Protestant and 1 as Protestant), and so we can imagine a one-unit change on this scale as being a movement from the first category to the second.
The only differences in the output would be the naming of the variable and - more importantly - that Standardised coefficients would also be calculated and displayed. Because in this case we have not labelled the values themselves (the two categories of the Protestantism variable have not been given labels, just the values 0 and 1), the naming of the output is actually cleaner when treating Protestantism as a “scale” type variable. This is common practice for dichotomous/binary/“dummy”/indicator variables, where the variable name “indicates” the case coded as 1 (here “Protestantism”; in the case of a variable categorising biological sex, we could name the variable itself as female and code males as 0 and females as 1).
The output from a regression in which we treat Protestantism as a “Scale” variable would look something like this:





It is often easier to treat dichotomous/“dummy”/indicator variables as “Scale” for modelling purposes. We can then calculate meaningful mean values for them and to standardise them to make them comparable with the scales of the other variables in the model. If we examine the regression results presented by Delhey and Newton (2005) in their Table 3, we realise that they actually report “Standardised” coefficients, meaning that all the predictor variables had been standardised before entered into the regression model.

title: Workshop 3 Worksheet
text:
You should now be well-equipped to reproduce and interpret the main regression models reported on in Table 3 in Delhey and Newton (2005) . The authors were interested in identifying the strongest predictors of national-level social trust and tested several potential explanatory variables. They found five that proved statistically significant (more on this later in Workshop 5) and robust across different models, and our delhey&newton2005 dataset contains all the relevant variables to reproduce these results. We should note that the dataset was compiled from a variety of sources described by the original authors in their article, but it is not the original dataset used by the authors themselves, so we should expect some differences compared to the published results.2 Nevertheless, the main results should be robust to these differences.
In this exercise, you have free hand to reproduce the four highlighted models from the article’s Table 3:







Source: Delhey and Newton (2005), p. 319



Questions

Which coefficients in the JASP output are the ones that match the coefficients reported in the article? Note that there are likely some differences in the actual numbers, but they should be still recognisably close to the published ones.
How do you interpret the results from these models?
What limitations in the analysis can you think of? What criticisms can you formulate?








TipSolution





The article reports standardised coefficients (with t-values in brackets) and the corrected R², so the matching numbers in JASP are in the Standardized column of the Coefficients table and the Adjusted R² column of the Model Summary (enter all predictors, including Protestantism, as Covariates). Our reconstructed dataset gives the following (n = 60, t-values in brackets), with the published figures for comparison:

How close are we? The pattern is the same as in the article: same signs, a similar ranking of the predictors, and adjusted R² values within 0.04 of the published ones. Our ethnic fractionalisation coefficients are a little weaker throughout, and in Model 3 it is not statistically significant (t = −1.64, p = .106), whereas the published one just is (t = −2.03, p < .05). Differences of this size are what a reconstructed dataset can produce.
Interpretation:

Model 1: Protestant tradition and ethnic fractionalisation alone account for about 44% of the cross-national variation in trust. In the unstandardized column, Protestant countries have about 22 percentage points higher trust than other countries with the same level of ethnic fractionalisation (b = 22.1). A one-SD higher ethnic fractionalisation (about 0.22 on its 0-1 scale) goes with about 0.31 SD (roughly 4.5 percentage points) lower trust, holding Protestantism constant. (A standardized coefficient for a 0/1 variable is harder to read, because one SD of Protestantism, 0.36, is not a meaningful difference between countries: this is why the unstandardized coefficient is often more useful for binary predictors.)
Models 3, 4 and 8 each add one more country characteristic. Better quality of government (+0.42), lower income inequality (−0.25) and higher national wealth (+0.32) are each associated with higher trust, over and above Protestantism and ethnic fractionalisation. Quality of government gives the biggest improvement (adjusted R² rises from 0.44 to 0.53).
Protestantism remains the strongest or second-strongest predictor in every model, but its coefficient shrinks when quality of government or national wealth is added (from 0.56 to 0.35 and 0.37). Part of the “Protestant” advantage is shared with good government and wealth: Protestant countries also tend to be richer and better governed.
Ethnic fractionalisation has a moderate negative association (−0.16 to −0.31) that also weakens once other characteristics are held constant.

Why separate models? Quality of government and national wealth are very highly correlated (r = 0.90). Entered together, their individual coefficients become unstable (VIFs of about 6) and the model cannot separate the two, which is why the authors add them one at a time.
Limitations and criticisms:

Only 60 countries, chosen because they took part in the World Values Survey, not at random.
One cross-section: the data cannot establish which comes first (does good government build trust, or does trust make good government possible?).
Country-level associations cannot be read as individual-level effects (the ecological fallacy).
Strong correlations among predictors make individual coefficients unstable, and which model one reports changes the story (e.g. how “important” Protestantism looks).
Measurement: trust is a single forced-choice question, and our dataset is a reconstruction from published sources, not the authors’ own data.

text:
Let’s look again at the assignment research questions. Some of these questions imply a dependent variable which is measured as a numeric scale or at least a long-ish (e.g. 7-point +) ordinal scale in one of the surveys we will use for the assignment (ESS10, WVS7, EVS2017). Other questions imply dependent variables that are more strictly categorical, and as such, we cannot model them using linear regression. For those, we may be able to apply another model type that better fits that kind of outcome variable (e.g. logistic regression), one of which we will be covering in Week 5.

title: Workshop 3 Worksheet
text:
Footnotes


By the way, a “quintile” (from the Latin word “quintus” for “five”) is simply a value that divides a scale into five equal parts - e.g. a scale of all the integers between 0 and 100 divided into five equal parts will contain 20 integers in each part, i.e. 100÷5↩︎
Some of the potentially most consequential sources of difference between the two datasets are the following: I could not find Ghana as a participating country in either the 1996 or 1990 World Values Survey; however, Malta was a participating country and also had useful measurements on all the other explanatory variables, so I have included it in the list of countries, making the dataset add up to 60, in line with the original sample size. Macro-economic data published by the World Bank or the OECD are often updated and corrected retrospectively, so if data for previous time periods are drawn form more recently published data releases, they may be slightly different than those available earlier. The categorisation of “Protestantism” is not described in too much detail by the authors, so it may be slightly different than the one done here (nonetheless, I have experimented with different possible options for coding it and the version included in the dataset was the most robust version). The finer details of the factor analysis used to compile the “Quality of government” scale were also not described by the authors, but the approach adopted here showed fit statistics that were close to those reported by the authors.↩︎

title: Week 5 Self-check Quiz: Uncertainty and inference
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 5 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. The examples use the same data as the lecture and Worksheet 5.


Why do we need confidence intervals and p-values at all?

Because survey data always contain mistakes
Because a different random sample would give a different estimate, and we want to say something about the population
Because JASP requires them
Because the mean is not reliable







TipAnswer





b. Every random sample gives a slightly different answer. Inference describes how far a single sample’s estimate is likely to be from the population value.






What happens to the standard error of a proportion if the sample size is four times larger?

It becomes four times smaller
It becomes about half as large
It stays the same
It becomes larger







TipAnswer





b. The standard error shrinks with the square root of the sample size: √4 = 2.






In the BSA 2010, 45.4% of 1,060 respondents say most people can be trusted (95% CI 42.3% to 48.4%). Which statement is correct?

95% of respondents gave an answer between 42.3% and 48.4%
We can be 95% confident that between 42.3% and 48.4% of British adults in 2010 would say most people can be trusted
The survey is 95% accurate
The true share is exactly 45.4%







TipAnswer





b. The interval gives a range of plausible values for the population share. It covers sampling error only, not problems with wording, non-response or coverage.






In a simulation, 50 random samples each produce a 95% confidence interval. About how many intervals would you expect to contain the true population value?

All 50
About 47 or 48
About 25
It’s impossible to say







TipAnswer





b. Across many samples, 95% of intervals built this way contain the true value (in the lecture’s simulation, 47 of 50). For any single real interval, we cannot know whether it is one of the hits or one of the misses.






An analyst claims that 20% of households are in poverty; your sample of 500 finds 23%. What is the null hypothesis?

The true share is 23%
The true share is 20%
The true share is not 20%
The sample is biased







TipAnswer





b. The null hypothesis is the “devil’s advocate” position: the claim is correct and our 23% differs from it only by chance.






For that poverty example, p = 0.09. What does this mean?

There is a 9% chance that the analyst is right
If the true share were 20%, samples of 500 at least this far from 20% would turn up about 9% of the time
The difference is 9 percentage points
We have proved the analyst is wrong







TipAnswer





b. The p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the null is true. At the conventional 5% level we would not reject the analyst’s claim, but that doesn’t prove it right either.






A regression coefficient has a 95% CI of −10.98 to −3.32. What can you say about its p-value?

It is below .05
It is above .05
It is exactly .05
Nothing: CIs and p-values are unrelated







TipAnswer





a. A 95% confidence interval excludes 0 exactly when the two-sided p-value is below .05. (This is the inequality coefficient in the Spirit Level model: p < .001.)






Men in the ESS score 0.27 points higher than women on the 0-10 trust scale (95% CI 0.05 to 0.49, p = .015; SD about 2.3). Which description is best?

A large and important gender gap
A statistically significant but small difference: about a tenth of a standard deviation
No real difference, because the gap is small
Men are 27% more trusting







TipAnswer





b. Statistical significance is about how surprising the data would be if there were no difference, not about how big the difference is. Always report the size of the difference and its interval.






In the BSA 2024, 16-24-year-olds score 0.16 points lower than older adults (95% CI −0.71 to 0.40, p = .58; only 78 young respondents). The much larger Community Life Survey finds a gap of −0.59. What should you conclude?

The BSA 2024 shows that young people’s trust is no different
The BSA 2024 is too imprecise to settle the question; its interval includes both 0 and −0.59
The two surveys contradict each other
The Community Life Survey must be wrong







TipAnswer





b. “Not statistically significant” means “not enough evidence”, not “no difference”. The BSA 2024 interval is compatible with no difference and with the CLS estimate.






In a logistic regression, the odds ratio for women is 0.65 with a 95% CI of 0.51 to 0.83. What does the interval tell you?

Women’s odds of trusting are lower than men’s, and the data are not compatible with no difference
The result is not statistically significant because the interval is wide
Women’s probability of trusting is between 51% and 83%
The interval should be checked against 0







TipAnswer





a. For odds ratios, “no difference” is 1, not 0. The whole interval lies below 1, so p < .05. The values are odds ratios, not probabilities.

title: Week 3 Self-check Quiz: Modelling continuous outcomes
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 3 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. Most examples use the Spirit Level data (pickett2009) from the lecture and Worksheet 3: trust is the percentage of people who say most people can be trusted; income inequality is the ratio of the income of the richest fifth to that of the poorest fifth.


The regression of trust on income inequality gives: predicted trust = 77.06 − 6.54 × inequality. What does −6.54 mean?

Trust falls by 6.54% in every country
Countries whose inequality ratio is one unit higher have, on average, 6.54 percentage points lower trust
Inequality explains 6.54% of trust
The correlation between inequality and trust is −6.54







TipAnswer





b. The slope is the average difference in the outcome per one-unit difference in the predictor, in the outcome’s own units.






What does the intercept, 77.06, describe here?

The average trust across the 23 countries
The predicted trust in a country with an inequality ratio of 0, which is impossible, so we don’t interpret it
The maximum possible trust
The trust of the most equal country







TipAnswer





b. The ratio can’t be below 1, so 0 lies far outside the data. The intercept is needed to draw the line but has no substantive meaning here. (The average trust, 38.8%, is the intercept of the null model M₀.)






Using predicted trust = 77.06 − 6.535 × inequality, what is the predicted trust for Portugal (inequality = 8)?

10.0%
24.8%
38.8%
52.3%







TipAnswer





b. 77.06 − 6.535 × 8 = 24.8%. Portugal’s observed trust is 10.0%, so its residual is 10.0 − 24.8 = −14.8 points.






What is a residual?

The part of the outcome explained by the predictor
The observed value minus the value predicted by the line
The slope of the line
A country with missing data







TipAnswer





b. Residuals are what the line gets wrong for each case. Least squares chooses the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible.






The model has R² = 0.44. What does this mean?

The slope is 0.44
Inequality accounts for 44% of the variation in trust across these countries
44% of countries are correctly predicted
Inequality causes 44% of a country’s trust







TipAnswer





b. R² is the share of the variation in the outcome that the model accounts for. The other 56% goes with other things. With one predictor, R² = r² (here (−0.664)² = 0.441).






In a model with both predictors, the coefficient for inequality is −7.15 and for homicides (per million) +0.17. Which conclusion is correct?

Inequality is 40 times more important than homicides
The coefficients are in different units, so their sizes can’t be compared directly; standardized coefficients or R² are needed
Homicides increase trust
Both predictors are equally important







TipAnswer





b. One unit of the inequality ratio and one homicide per million people are not comparable units. Standardized coefficients express both in standard deviations. (And c is wrong twice: the homicide coefficient is tiny and uncertain, and “increase” is causal language.)






What does “adjusting for homicide rates” mean for the inequality coefficient in a multiple regression?

Homicides were removed from the data
The coefficient describes the association between inequality and trust among countries with the same homicide rate
We have proved that homicides don’t affect trust
We ran an experiment that held homicides fixed







TipAnswer





b. Multiple regression compares like with like statistically. It is not an experiment, and it only adjusts for the variables actually in the model.






In a regression of trust on world region with Western Europe as the reference category, the intercept is 40.66 and the coefficient for Asia is −13.96. What is the predicted trust for an Asian country?

−13.96%
13.96%
26.70%
54.62%







TipAnswer





c. 40.66 − 13.96 = 26.70%, which is simply the mean of the Asian countries. Each region’s coefficient is its difference from the reference category.






Protestant countries have mean trust of 48.26% and other countries 24.81%. In a regression of trust on Protestantism (coded 1 = Protestant, 0 = not), what is the coefficient?

24.81
48.26
23.45
0.36







TipAnswer





c. With a single 0/1 predictor, the coefficient is the difference between the two group means (48.26 − 24.81). The intercept (24.81) is the mean of the group coded 0.






Which of these is not a good reason to doubt a regression line?

The scatter plot shows a curved pattern
One extreme case tilts the line
Two predictors are almost perfectly correlated (high VIF)
The R² is below 0.5







TipAnswer





d. A modest R² is normal in social science and does not make the line wrong: it just means other factors matter too. Curvature (Anscombe’s quartet), influential cases and multicollinearity are genuine reasons for caution.

text:

Trust falls by 6.54% in every country

Inequality explains 6.54% of trust
The correlation between inequality and trust is −6.54







TipAnswer





b. The slope is the average difference in the outcome per one-unit difference in the predictor, in the outcome’s own units.

title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 1 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. The examples use the same data as the lecture and Worksheet 1 (mainly the UK sample of the European Social Survey 2023-24, gb-ess11-trust.sav).


Which level of measurement is age in years (agea)?

Nominal
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio







TipAnswer





d. Age has equal steps between values and a true zero, so ratios make sense (a 60-year-old is twice as old as a 30-year-old). In JASP, interval and ratio variables are both treated as Scale.






Which summary makes sense for a nominal variable such as sex (gndr)?

The mean
The median
The mode and the percentage in each category
The standard deviation







TipAnswer





c. Nominal categories have no order, so only counts, percentages and the mode are meaningful. JASP will happily calculate a “mean” of the codes 1 and 2, but it means nothing.






For trust in the ESS (0-10), the mean is 5.40, the median 6 and the mode 7. What does this pattern suggest?

The distribution is perfectly symmetric
A tail of low scores pulls the mean below the median (mild left skew)
A few very high scores pull the mean up (right skew)
The data contain errors







TipAnswer





b. More people answer above the middle of the scale than below, but a tail of very low answers (0 to 2, chosen by 13% of respondents) drags the mean down. In a right-skewed distribution such as income, it’s the other way round: the mean is above the median.






Nine households have incomes (in £000s) of 18, 22, 25, 28, 31, 34, 38, 45 and 400. Which figure best describes a “typical” household?

The mean, 71
The median, 31
The range, 382
The maximum, 400







TipAnswer





b. The single very high income pulls the mean (71) above eight of the nine households. The median (31) is barely affected, which is why incomes and wealth are usually reported as medians.






In the BSA 2010, 484 respondents said “most people can be trusted”, out of 3,297 people in the file. Only 1,081 were asked the question, and 17 of them answered “Don’t know” or refused. Which percentage best describes the share of trusting answers?

484 / 3,297 = 14.7%
484 / 1,081 = 44.8%
484 / 1,064 = 45.5%
All three are equally good







TipAnswer





c. The question was only asked in one version of the questionnaire, so the 2,216 people never asked must be left out of the denominator. “Don’t know” and refusals are not substantive answers either, so the clearest figure uses the 1,064 substantive answers. Always check what the denominator of a percentage is.






In the BSA 2010, 484 respondents said “most people can be trusted” and 580 said “you can’t be too careful”. What is the ratio of trusting to careful answers?

0.45
0.83
1.20
45.5%







TipAnswer





b. 484 ÷ 580 = 0.83: about 8 trusting answers for every 10 careful ones. (0.45 is the proportion trusting, and 1.20 is the ratio the other way round.) In Week 4 this ratio reappears as the odds of trusting.






The standard deviation of trust in the ESS is 2.30. What does it describe?

The typical respondent’s trust score
The typical distance of an answer from the mean
The difference between the highest and lowest answers
The share of respondents within one point of the mean







TipAnswer





b. A typical answer lies about 2.3 points above or below the mean of 5.4. The difference between the highest and lowest answers is the range (here 10).






In a box plot of ESS trust, the box runs from 4 to 7 and the line inside it is at 6. What do these numbers show?

The minimum, maximum and mean
The 25th percentile, the 75th percentile and the median
The mean ± one standard deviation
The two most common answers and the average







TipAnswer





b. The box covers the middle 50% of respondents (the interquartile range, 7 − 4 = 3), and the line marks the median.






Six British surveys asked about trust in “most people”. Depending on the survey, the share giving a trusting answer ranged from about 37% to 48% (11 percentage points apart), and two 0-10 scales had means of 4.3 and 6.1. What is the main lesson?

Trust changed dramatically between surveys
One of the surveys must have made an error
Question wording, answer options and survey design shape the measured level of trust
Social trust cannot be measured







TipAnswer





c. The surveys word the question differently, offer different answer options (two options, a middle category, an unoffered “depends”, 0-10 scales with different labels), use different modes and cover different populations. Levels of trust should only be compared across surveys with great care; comparisons within one survey are much safer.






In the BSA 2024 file, the 0-10 trust question has the extra values 12 (“Can’t choose”) and 99 (“Prefer not to answer”), which are not defined as missing. What happens if you calculate the mean straight away?

Nothing: JASP ignores non-answers automatically
The mean is too high, because 12 and 99 are averaged in as if they were scores
The mean is too low
JASP refuses to calculate a mean







TipAnswer





b. Unless they are set as missing, JASP treats 12 and 99 as valid values and includes them in the mean. Always look at a frequency table, compare values with labels, and set non-answers as missing first (Workshop 4 shows how).

title: Interpretation Guide: Saying What Your Results Mean
text:
For each kind of output you will meet in this module, this guide gives:

what to look at in the JASP output,
a model write-up you can adapt for your own report, and
common phrasings to avoid, with better alternatives.

All the examples use the course datasets, so you can reproduce every number yourself.






ImportantThree rules for every write-up




Say what was measured: name the survey, year, question and scale, not just the variable name.
Give direction and size: “higher” is not enough. Say how much higher, in units a reader understands.
Describe associations, not causes: regression on survey data shows how variables go together. Use “is associated with”, “is higher among”, “predicts”, not “causes”, “increases”, “leads to” or “the effect of”.





Example: social trust (ppltrst, 0-10) in the UK sample of the European Social Survey, Round 11 (gb-ess11-trust.sav).
Look at: valid N, mean, median, mode, standard deviation, and the distribution plot.

In the UK sample of the European Social Survey (2023-24, n = 1,680), respondents rated how far most people can be trusted at 5.4 on average on a scale from 0 (“you can’t be too careful”) to 10 (“most people can be trusted”) (SD = 2.3). The median was 6 and the most common answer 7, so more respondents leaned towards trust than away from it, with a smaller tail of very low scores pulling the mean slightly below the median.








✗ Avoid
✓ Better




“The mean of ppltrst is 5.4.”
Name the concept and the scale: “average trust was 5.4 on a 0-10 scale”.


“Most people trust others.”
Say what the numbers show: “the most common answer was 7 out of 10”.


Reporting the mean of a nominal variable
Use percentages and the mode for categorical variables.






Example: SocTrust by sex, British Social Attitudes 2010 (column percentages).




Men
Women

Look at: percentages within each category of the predictor (column percentages if the predictor is in the columns), and the size of the difference.

In the 2010 British Social Attitudes survey, men were more likely than women to say that most people can be trusted (51% vs 41%), a difference of about 11 percentage points.








✗ Avoid
✓ Better




“237 men and 244 women trust people.”
Compare percentages, not counts: the groups are different sizes.


“Women are 11% less trusting.”
“11 percentage points lower” (40.7% is about 21% lower than 51.4%: not the same thing).


Using row percentages to compare men and women
Percentages must add to 100 within each group you compare.






Example: ppltrst (0-10) by gender, ESS Round 11, UK.
Look at: the mean or median in each group, the spread, and the box plot.

Men in the UK ESS sample reported slightly higher trust than women (mean 5.5 vs 5.3 on the 0-10 scale; medians 6 and 5). The distributions overlap heavily: the gap between the group means is small compared with the spread within each group (SD of about 2.3 points).




Example: income inequality and social trust across 23 rich countries (pickett2009).
Look at: the scatter plot first, then Pearson’s r (direction and strength).

Across 23 economically developed countries, income inequality and social trust were strongly negatively correlated (r = −0.66): in more unequal countries, a smaller share of people said that most people can be trusted.








✗ Avoid
✓ Better




“Inequality reduces trust.”
“Inequality is negatively associated with trust.”


“Unequal countries have untrusting citizens.”
The data are country-level: they describe countries, not individuals (the ecological fallacy).


“r = −0.66, so 66% of trust is explained.”
The share of variance explained is r² ≈ 0.44.






Example: Trust (% trusting) regressed on Income inequality (income quintile share ratio), pickett2009.

Look at: the Unstandardized coefficient of the predictor, in the units of both variables; R².

A simple linear regression shows that countries with higher income inequality tend to have lower social trust: each one-unit higher income quintile share ratio (for example, the richest fifth earning 8 rather than 7 times as much as the poorest fifth) is associated with a share of trusting people that is about 6.5 percentage points lower. Income inequality alone accounts for 44% of the variation in trust across these countries (R² = 0.44).

The intercept (77.06) is the predicted trust when inequality is 0, which is impossible (the ratio cannot be below 1), so it does not need interpreting.

Look at: how the main coefficient changes once controls are added; each coefficient’s CI and p-value; R².

Adjusting for homicide rates, income inequality remained negatively associated with trust: among countries with similar homicide rates, a one-unit higher quintile share ratio was associated with about 7 percentage points lower trust (95% CI −11.0 to −3.3; p < .001). Homicide rates were not reliably associated with trust once inequality was taken into account (b = 0.17, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.68; p = .48), and adding them improved the model’s explanatory power only marginally (R² from 0.44 to 0.46).








✗ Avoid
✓ Better

“Homicides increase trust (b = 0.17).”
The CI includes 0 and p = .48: the data cannot tell the direction of this association.


“Inequality matters more because −7.15 > 0.17.”
The variables have different units: compare standardized coefficients for relative strength.

Look at: which category is the reference; each coefficient is a difference from it.

Adults aged 16-24 rated their trust in most people 0.6 points lower on the 0-10 scale than those aged 25 and over, holding sex constant (95% CI −0.65 to −0.53; p < .001). There was no meaningful difference between men and women.

Look at: which outcome category is coded 1; the Odds Ratio column; then translate into predicted probabilities (conditional estimates plot).

A logistic regression shows that, among respondents of the same age, women had about 35% lower odds than men of saying that most people can be trusted (OR = 0.65, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.83; p < .001). In probability terms, the model predicts that 50% of 40-year-old men but 39% of 40-year-old women say most people can be trusted, a gap of about 11 percentage points that is similar at every age. Older respondents were slightly more trusting (about 0.6% higher odds per year of age, or 6% per decade), but this association was not statistically significant (95% CI 0.9995 to 1.013, which JASP rounds to 1.000; p = .069). Age and sex together explain very little of the variation in trust (Nagelkerke R² = 0.02).








✗ Avoid
✓ Better




“Women are 35% less likely to trust.”
“Women’s odds of trusting are 35% lower”, and give the probability gap (11 points).


“The odds ratio is 0.646, so women’s probability is 0.646.”
Odds ratios compare odds, not probabilities.


Interpreting the log-odds Estimate directly as a size
Use the sign of the Estimate for direction; use the odds ratio or probabilities for size.


Not saying which category is coded 1
“The outcome is coded 1 for ‘most people can be trusted’.”






Look at: the 95% CI (the range of population values compatible with the data) and the p-value (how surprising the estimate would be if the true association were zero).

The odds of trusting were 35% lower for women (OR = 0.65, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.83; p < .001). Because the interval lies entirely below 1, the data are not compatible with the absence of a sex difference in the population.

A non-significant result is not evidence of no difference. In the British Social Attitudes 2024, 16-24-year-olds scored 0.16 points lower than older adults on the 0-10 trust scale (95% CI −0.71 to 0.40; p = .58), based on only 78 young respondents.

The BSA 2024 shows a small difference in the same direction that is not statistically significant. Its confidence interval is wide and includes both no difference and the 0.6-point gap found in the much larger Community Life Survey, so the BSA 2024 cannot settle whether young people’s trust is lower.








✗ Avoid
✓ Better




“p = .58, so there is no difference.”
“The difference is not statistically significant; the interval is compatible with no difference and with a sizeable one.”


“p < .001, so the effect is large.”
Significance is about precision, not size: report the coefficient and its interval.


“There is a 95% probability that the true value is in the CI.”
“Intervals built this way capture the true value in 95% of repeated samples.”


“p = 0.000”
Report “p < .001”.






Before you submit, check that each model you report states:

the data source, year, population and sample size (n)
how the outcome was measured and coded (for logistic regression: which category is 1)
any recoding decisions (missing values, collapsed categories, cut-points) and why
the reference category of every categorical predictor
the direction and size of each key association, in meaningful units
a 95% CI and/or p-value for each key estimate
a measure of model fit (R² or a pseudo-R²)
associational, not causal, language
limitations: measurement, sample (coverage, size, weights) and design (cross-sectional data)

title: Interpretation Guide: Saying What Your Results Mean

Example: social trust (ppltrst, 0-10) in the UK sample of the European Social Survey, Round 11 (gb-ess11-trust.sav).

text:

Look at: the scatter plot first, then Pearson’s r (direction and strength).

Across 23 economically developed countries, income inequality and social trust were strongly negatively correlated (r = −0.66): in more unequal countries, a smaller share of people said that most people can be trusted.

✓ Better

Look at: which outcome category is coded 1; the Odds Ratio column; then translate into predicted probabilities (conditional estimates plot).

A logistic regression shows that, among respondents of the same age, women had about 35% lower odds than men of saying that most people can be trusted (OR = 0.65, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.83; p < .001). In probability terms, the model predicts that 50% of 40-year-old men but 39% of 40-year-old women say most people can be trusted, a gap of about 11 percentage points that is similar at every age. Older respondents were slightly more trusting (about 0.6% higher odds per year of age, or 6% per decade), but this association was not statistically significant (95% CI 0.9995 to 1.013, which JASP rounds to 1.000; p = .069). Age and sex together explain very little of the variation in trust (Nagelkerke R² = 0.02).








✗ Avoid
✓ Better




“Women are 35% less likely to trust.”
“Women’s odds of trusting are 35% lower”, and give the probability gap (11 points).


“The odds ratio is 0.646, so women’s probability is 0.646.”
Odds ratios compare odds, not probabilities.


Interpreting the log-odds Estimate directly as a size
Use the sign of the Estimate for direction; use the odds ratio or probabilities for size.


Not saying which category is coded 1
“The outcome is coded 1 for ‘most people can be trusted’.”

title: Interpretation Guide: Saying What Your Results Mean
text:
Look at: the 95% CI (the range of population values compatible with the data) and the p-value (how surprising the estimate would be if the true association were zero).

The odds of trusting were 35% lower for women (OR = 0.65, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.83; p < .001). Because the interval lies entirely below 1, the data are not compatible with the absence of a sex difference in the population.

A non-significant result is not evidence of no difference. In the British Social Attitudes 2024, 16-24-year-olds scored 0.16 points lower than older adults on the 0-10 trust scale (95% CI −0.71 to 0.40; p = .58), based on only 78 young respondents.

The BSA 2024 shows a small difference in the same direction that is not statistically significant. Its confidence interval is wide and includes both no difference and the 0.6-point gap found in the much larger Community Life Survey, so the BSA 2024 cannot settle whether young people’s trust is lower.








✗ Avoid
✓ Better




“p = .58, so there is no difference.”
“The difference is not statistically significant; the interval is compatible with no difference and with a sizeable one.”


“p < .001, so the effect is large.”
Significance is about precision, not size: report the coefficient and its interval.


“There is a 95% probability that the true value is in the CI.”
“Intervals built this way capture the true value in 95% of repeated samples.”


“p = 0.000”
Report “p < .001”.

title: Interpretation Guide: Saying What Your Results Mean
text:
Before you submit, check that each model you report states:

the data source, year, population and sample size (n)
how the outcome was measured and coded (for logistic regression: which category is 1)
any recoding decisions (missing values, collapsed categories, cut-points) and why
the reference category of every categorical predictor
the direction and size of each key association, in meaningful units
a 95% CI and/or p-value for each key estimate
a measure of model fit (R² or a pseudo-R²)
associational, not causal, language
limitations: measurement, sample (coverage, size, weights) and design (cross-sectional data)

“Intervals built this way capture the true value in 95% of repeated samples.”


“p = 0.000”
Report “p < .001”.

title: Interpretation Guide: Saying What Your Results Mean
text:
Before you submit, check that each model you report states:

the data source, year, population and sample size (n)
how the outcome was measured and coded (for logistic regression: which category is 1)
any recoding decisions (missing values, collapsed categories, cut-points) and why
the reference category of every categorical predictor
the direction and size of each key association, in meaningful units
a 95% CI and/or p-value for each key estimate
a measure of model fit (R² or a pseudo-R²)
associational, not causal, language
limitations: measurement, sample (coverage, size, weights) and design (cross-sectional data)

title: Week 2 Self-check Quiz: Comparisons and associations
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 2 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. The examples use the same data as the lecture and Worksheet 2.


You want to describe how trust on the ESS 0-10 scale differs between men and women. Which tool fits?

A contingency table with row percentages
Group means and medians, shown in box plots
A scatter plot with a correlation
A frequency table of trust







TipAnswer





b. One variable is categorical (sex) and one is treated as scale (trust), so we compare the distribution of trust across the groups. Contingency tables are for two categorical variables; scatter plots for two scale variables.






In a study of age and social trust, which variable is the outcome?

Age
Social trust
Either, it makes no difference
Neither: both are explanatory







TipAnswer





b. Age can plausibly shape trust, but trust cannot change someone’s age. For many pairs (e.g. volunteering and trust) the direction is less obvious, and theory has to decide.






In the BSA 2010, 51.7% of men and 40.7% of women say most people can be trusted. These are column percentages with sex in the columns. What question do they answer?

What share of trusting respondents are men?
Are men or women more likely to say most people can be trusted?
How many respondents trust most people?
Is the difference statistically significant?







TipAnswer





b. Column percentages compare the groups in the columns: men are about 11 percentage points more likely to trust. Row percentages would answer question a (and only describe who the trusting are, which depends on how many men and women were sampled).






Trust is 51.7% among men and 40.7% among women. Which description is correct?

Women are 11% less trusting
Women are 11 percentage points less likely to trust
Women are 21% as trusting as men
The gap is 0.11%







TipAnswer





b. The difference between two percentages is measured in percentage points. In relative terms, 40.7% is about 21% lower than 51.7%, which is a different statement: always say which one you mean.






In the ESS, the box plots of trust for men and women both run from 4 to 7, with medians of 6 (men) and 5 (women). What can you conclude?

Men and women have identical trust
Men trust slightly more on average, but the two distributions overlap almost completely
All men trust more than all women
Women’s trust varies more because their median is lower







TipAnswer





b. The middle 50% of both groups covers the same range; only the medians (and the means, 5.54 vs 5.27) differ slightly. A gap between groups should always be judged against the spread within them.






The correlation between income inequality and trust across 23 rich countries is r = −0.66. What does it mean?

Inequality causes 66% of the variation in trust
More unequal countries tend to have lower trust, and the association is fairly strong
Every unequal country has low trust
66% of countries are unequal







TipAnswer





b. The sign gives the direction (negative: higher inequality, lower trust) and the size gives the strength. There are clear exceptions (e.g. the USA and New Zealand trust more than their inequality would suggest), and a correlation says nothing about cause.






A scatter plot shows a clear U-shaped relationship, yet Pearson’s r is almost exactly 0. Why?

There must be an error in the calculation
r only measures straight-line (linear) association
r is always close to zero for curves with many points
The two variables are unrelated







TipAnswer





b. Pearson’s r captures linear association only. That’s why you should always look at the scatter plot before relying on a correlation.






In the 2024 Spirit Level data (43 countries), the correlation between the income quintile ratio and trust is −0.15, but −0.58 without China. What does this show?

China’s data must be wrong
One unusual case can change a correlation a lot
The 2024 data contradict the 2009 data
The quintile ratio is not a measure of inequality







TipAnswer





b. China combines by far the highest measured inequality with high measured trust, which flattens the line. Look for unusual cases in the scatter plot and report how much they matter.






Unequal countries tend to have lower trust. Can we conclude that poorer individuals trust less?

Yes, that’s what the correlation means
No: country-level data describe countries, not individuals
Yes, if the correlation is strong enough
No, because the correlation is negative







TipAnswer





b. Drawing conclusions about individuals from group-level data is the ecological fallacy. To study individuals we need individual-level survey data.






Which of these explanations for the inequality-trust correlation can the correlation itself rule out?

Inequality erodes trust
Trust reduces inequality (trusting societies support redistribution)
Something else, such as history or institutions, drives both
None of them







TipAnswer





d. A correlation is compatible with all three stories. To weigh them we need theory, other variables (Week 3: multiple regression lets us adjust for some third factors) and ideally data over time.

title: Week 4 Self-check Quiz: Modelling dichotomous outcomes
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 4 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. The examples use the same data as the lecture and Worksheet 4 (British Social Attitudes 2010: SocTrust modelled on age and sex).


Which of these outcome variables calls for logistic rather than linear regression?

Trust in most people, measured on a 0-10 scale (ESS ppltrst)
The percentage of a country’s population who say most people can be trusted
Whether the respondent voted in the last general election (yes/no)
The number of close friends a respondent has







TipAnswer





c. It has only two possible values, so we model the probability of “yes”. The 0-10 scale (a) and the country percentage (b) can be treated as numeric scales; a count (d) is numeric too.






30% of a sample say most people can be trusted. What are the odds of trusting?

0.30
0.43
2.33
0.70







TipAnswer





b. Odds = p ÷ (1 − p) = 0.3 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 0.43, or 3 trusting for every 7 who are not. (2.33 is the odds of not trusting.)






A logistic regression Estimate is 0. What does that mean?

The predicted probability is 0
The odds ratio is 1: the predictor makes no difference to the odds
The predictor perfectly predicts the outcome
Nobody in the sample is in the category coded 1







TipAnswer





b. Estimates are on the log-odds scale, and e⁰ = 1. An odds ratio of 1 means the odds are the same whatever the value of the predictor.






JASP reports an Estimate of 0.693 for a predictor Sex (Female). What is the odds ratio, and what does it mean?

0.693: women’s odds are about 31% lower than men’s
2.0: women’s odds are twice men’s
1.693: women are 69% more likely than men to be in the outcome category
You cannot tell without the p-value







TipAnswer





b. The odds ratio is e0.693 ≈ 2.0, so women’s odds are about twice men’s. Option c confuses odds with probability (and uses the wrong conversion). JASP shows the Odds Ratio column by default, so you rarely need to do this by hand.






In the BSA 2010 model, Sex (Female) has an odds ratio of 0.646. Which statement is correct?

Women are 35% less likely than men to say most people can be trusted
Among people of the same age, women’s odds of trusting are about 35% lower than men’s
The probability that a woman trusts most people is 0.646
Being a woman causes lower trust







TipAnswer





b. (0.646 − 1) × 100 = −35%, and this is a change in odds, adjusted for age. Statement a describes probabilities, which differ by about 11 percentage points (see Question 9). Statement d makes a causal claim that survey data alone cannot support.






When you first fit the BSA 2010 model, JASP notes that “Can’t be too careful in dealing with people” has been coded as class 1. What does the model describe?

The probability of trusting most people
The probability of not trusting most people
Nothing: JASP fixes the coding automatically
The mean of SocTrust







TipAnswer





b. Logistic regression models the probability of the category coded 1, and JASP codes the second category as 1. All coefficients would flip sign. Reverse the label order (or recode) so that 1 = “Most people can be trusted”.






You need to dichotomise a 1-5 trust scale, and the most common answer is the unlabelled middle value, 3. What is the best practice?

Always group the middle value with the higher values
Try both cut-points and report the one with the smaller p-value
Choose the cut on conceptual grounds before seeing the results, report it, and check whether a reasonable alternative changes the conclusions
Drop everyone who answered 3







TipAnswer





c. In the BSA 2010 self-completion question, the conclusions about age and sex flip depending on where the 3s go (Worksheet 4, Exercise 4.1.1). Choosing the cut by its p-value (b) is a form of p-hacking; dropping a quarter of the sample (d) throws away data and changes who you are studying.






The BSA 2010 model with age and sex has a Nagelkerke R² of 0.019. Which reading is right?

Age and sex together account for only a very small share of the variation in trust
The model explains 19% of the variation in trust
The coefficients for age and sex are not statistically significant
The model has been fitted incorrectly







TipAnswer





a. Pseudo-R² measures like Nagelkerke’s are rough guides, but 0.019 is very small. A small R² is common for attitudes and does not mean the coefficients are wrong or non-significant: the sex coefficient has p < .001.






The model predicts that a 20-year-old man has a 47% probability of saying most people can be trusted, and a 20-year-old woman 36%. How big is the sex difference in probability terms?

35%
About 11 percentage points
0.646
1.98







TipAnswer





b. 47% − 36% ≈ 11 percentage points, and the gap is similar at every age. This is the clearest way to tell a general reader how big the difference is. The 35% (a) and 0.646 (c) describe odds, not probabilities.






If you fit a linear regression to the 0/1 SocTrust outcome with age and sex, the coefficient for Sex (Female) is −0.108. What does it mean?

Women are about 10.8 percentage points less likely than men of the same age to say most people can be trusted
Women’s odds of trusting are 10.8% lower
The log-odds of trusting are 0.108 lower for women
Women are 0.108 times as likely to trust







TipAnswer





a. With a 0/1 outcome, a linear regression coefficient is a difference in probability. Here it almost exactly matches the logistic model’s predictions, because all the predicted probabilities sit between 35% and 60%, where the logistic curve is close to a straight line.

Nobody in the sample is in the category coded 1







TipAnswer





b. Estimates are on the log-odds scale, and e⁰ = 1. An odds ratio of 1 means the odds are the same whatever the value of the predictor.

title: Week 4 Self-check Quiz: Modelling dichotomous outcomes
text:
JASP reports an Estimate of 0.693 for a predictor Sex (Female). What is the odds ratio, and what does it mean?

0.693: women’s odds are about 31% lower than men’s
2.0: women’s odds are twice men’s
1.693: women are 69% more likely than men to be in the outcome category
You cannot tell without the p-value







TipAnswer





b. The odds ratio is e0.693 ≈ 2.0, so women’s odds are about twice men’s. Option c confuses odds with probability (and uses the wrong conversion). JASP shows the Odds Ratio column by default, so you rarely need to do this by hand.

title: Week 4 Self-check Quiz: Modelling dichotomous outcomes
text:
In the BSA 2010 model, Sex (Female) has an odds ratio of 0.646. Which statement is correct?

Women are 35% less likely than men to say most people can be trusted
Among people of the same age, women’s odds of trusting are about 35% lower than men’s
The probability that a woman trusts most people is 0.646
Being a woman causes lower trust







TipAnswer





b. (0.646 − 1) × 100 = −35%, and this is a change in odds, adjusted for age. Statement a describes probabilities, which differ by about 11 percentage points (see Question 9). Statement d makes a causal claim that survey data alone cannot support.

title: Week 4 Self-check Quiz: Modelling dichotomous outcomes
text:
When you first fit the BSA 2010 model, JASP notes that “Can’t be too careful in dealing with people” has been coded as class 1. What does the model describe?

The probability of trusting most people
The probability of not trusting most people
Nothing: JASP fixes the coding automatically
The mean of SocTrust







TipAnswer





b. Logistic regression models the probability of the category coded 1, and JASP codes the second category as 1. All coefficients would flip sign. Reverse the label order (or recode) so that 1 = “Most people can be trusted”.

title: Week 4 Self-check Quiz: Modelling dichotomous outcomes
text:
You need to dichotomise a 1-5 trust scale, and the most common answer is the unlabelled middle value, 3. What is the best practice?

Always group the middle value with the higher values
Try both cut-points and report the one with the smaller p-value
Choose the cut on conceptual grounds before seeing the results, report it, and check whether a reasonable alternative changes the conclusions
Drop everyone who answered 3







TipAnswer





c. In the BSA 2010 self-completion question, the conclusions about age and sex flip depending on where the 3s go (Worksheet 4, Exercise 4.1.1). Choosing the cut by its p-value (b) is a form of p-hacking; dropping a quarter of the sample (d) throws away data and changes who you are studying.

title: Week 4 Self-check Quiz: Modelling dichotomous outcomes
text:
The BSA 2010 model with age and sex has a Nagelkerke R² of 0.019. Which reading is right?

Age and sex together account for only a very small share of the variation in trust
The model explains 19% of the variation in trust
The coefficients for age and sex are not statistically significant
The model has been fitted incorrectly







TipAnswer





a. Pseudo-R² measures like Nagelkerke’s are rough guides, but 0.019 is very small. A small R² is common for attitudes and does not mean the coefficients are wrong or non-significant: the sex coefficient has p < .001.

title: Week 4 Self-check Quiz: Modelling dichotomous outcomes
text:
The model predicts that a 20-year-old man has a 47% probability of saying most people can be trusted, and a 20-year-old woman 36%. How big is the sex difference in probability terms?

35%
About 11 percentage points
0.646
1.98







TipAnswer





b. 47% − 36% ≈ 11 percentage points, and the gap is similar at every age. This is the clearest way to tell a general reader how big the difference is. The 35% (a) and 0.646 (c) describe odds, not probabilities.

title: Week 4 Self-check Quiz: Modelling dichotomous outcomes
text:
If you fit a linear regression to the 0/1 SocTrust outcome with age and sex, the coefficient for Sex (Female) is −0.108. What does it mean?

Women are about 10.8 percentage points less likely than men of the same age to say most people can be trusted
Women’s odds of trusting are 10.8% lower
The log-odds of trusting are 0.108 lower for women
Women are 0.108 times as likely to trust







TipAnswer





a. With a 0/1 outcome, a linear regression coefficient is a difference in probability. Here it almost exactly matches the logistic model’s predictions, because all the predicted probabilities sit between 35% and 60%, where the logistic curve is close to a straight line.

title: Workshop 1 Worksheet
text:
The lecture has introduced the complexities of measuring sociological concepts. Throughout this short course, we will be using the measurement and estimation of social trust as a guiding example. However, the aim is to help you build up your skills and confidence in asking and addressing research questions of your own, and the assessment questions will ask you to analyse some other chosen research topic.
In this first workshop, you will begin your data analysis journey by exploring some online sources of cross-national sociological data available for secondary analysis, and you will practice performing basic descriptive analyses of selected variables.



By the end of the session you will have gained familiarity with:

some important UK-focused and international survey programmes and freely available data sources
the challenges of measuring sociological concepts using surveys
the basics of using a statistical data analysis software package: JASP




Create a folder to store your data for this module on your institutional OneDrive platform (e.g. C:\OneDrive - Newcastle University\SOC2069). Within that folder, create a sub-folder called “Data”. You will then be able to save data files and documentation as you progress.



About 30 minutes
The lecture has introduced some elementary concepts of descriptive statistics. In this first exercise we will practice performing univariate descriptive statistics using a statistical software package called JASP.


As a first step, we need to find some data to explore. We will be using a number of small datasets that can be downloaded from the Data page. On that page, you can roll down the first section called Questions of Trust and find the download button.
Under the Questions of Trust section you will find a collection of six small datasets compiled from original sources to exemplify several different ways in which the “social trust” / “generalised trust” question has been asked in social surveys. The datasets are helpful for thinking through questions about concept measurement similar to those asked by Bekkers and Sandberg (2019).
The focus of the datasets is on a single country: Great Britain / United Kingdom. The original datasets have been reduced to a small number of variables: (1) respondent ID number; (2) questionnaire subsample (if relevant and available); (3) age (both numeric and categorical (7 categories) where available); (4) sex; (5) and social trust. The order of the variables in the dataset, variable names and labels, and value/category codes and labels - including missing values - were left as in the original surveys (the only exception is the gb-cls23-trust_nm dataset, where the missing values have been excluded due to the large size of the original file - over 100,000 rows - which cannot be opened by JASP). The datasets can be downloaded in .sav (SPSS) format and loaded directly in JASP or R.
The available datasets and their original sources are:

British Social Attitudes Survey 2024 (gb-bsa24-trust.sav)
British Social Attitudes Survey 2023 (gb-bsa23-trust.sav)
British Social Attitudes Survey 2010 (gb-bsa10-trust.sav)
Community Life Survey 2023-24 (gb-cls23-trust_nm.sav)
Citizenship Survey 2010-11 (gb-cs10-trust.sav)
European Social Survey, Round 11, 2023-24 (UK sample) (gb-ess11-trust.sav)

You can download each dataset to the “Data” folder you created in Exercise 0 earlier, so you have them in your local folder to practice basic descriptive statistics in JASP using them. As we will only be using these datasets in this workshop, it may be a clean approach to create another sub-folder for this week (e.g. “w1) and store the datasets there.
But in this exercise, you will use gb-ess11-trust.sav as a worked-out example, so make sure that one is downloaded!






ImportantDO NOT just click on the downloaded files!



The dataset files you have just downloaded come in .sav format, which is a proprietary format for another software package (SPSS). Many social survey datasets are made available in this or similar formats. JASP can import these formats and make them usable within the software, but if you directly click on the downloaded files, if other software are available on the computer – and SPSS generally is –, then the datasets will open in that other software by default. If that happens, just close the windows that have opened and follow the guidance in Task 2 below.





Open the JASP software from the Start menu. If you are using your own laptop, you can install the latest version of JASP from https://jasp-stats.org/.
The opening page should look something like this:





To open a dataset stored on your computer, you can navigate to the three horizontal bars (“hamburger”) menu icon > Open > Computer > Browse.





In JASP you can work on one dataset at a time (or in one window), but you can open several datasets in separate JASP instances/windows. For now, work with one dataset. When you finish your analysis, you can save both the dataset and the outputs you generated as one .jasp file, which you can then open later and continue or alter your analyses.
Open the gb-ess11-trust.sav dataset. You should now see something like this:





You can scroll up-down and left-right in the dataset to have a look at the spreadsheet and its contents. In this case, the dataset is very small, only contains four variables, so there is no need to scroll horizontally to inspect variables as it all fits on the screen.



What we see is the “analysis view”, the main window that we will be using to perform analyses. We can also manually edit our data if we ever need to by clicking on the “Edit Data” tab:





That will take us to the “data view”, which is a dangerous place to be because we can manually alter our data, maybe even involuntarily. We will often need to perform changes to our data, but for now we can return to the analysis view window by clicking on the “Analyses” tab:








We will explore some descriptive statistics using the Descriptives > Descriptive Statistics menu option. If you click through, you should see something like this:


















Step 1: Identify the variable referring to “social/generalised trust” and move that variable to the Variables field
Step 2: Under Tables, select Frequency tables and set the Maximum distinct values to a much higher number (e.g. 100 - this latter step is only needed because the ppltrst variable has 11 valid categories and the default maximum number of distinct values for Frequency tables to be produced is 10. This default setting is reasonable, given that it is difficult to read off too much useful information from a long frequency table, as we will see in the output):





Step 3: Under Basic plots select Distribution plots as well





Now check the output that was automatically generated in the panel on the right and interpret the results; use the guiding questions below

Questions

How many levels (categories) does the variable have in your dataset? Is it what you had expected based on the questionnaire information from the lecture slides?
Does the variable have any missing values in your dataset?
What is the “Mode” of the variable, and what does that mean?
What percentage of the respondents in your dataset had answered that “Most people can be trusted”?
What is the most common answer category, and what do these descriptive statistics tell you about social trust in this sample?
Is this “social trust” variable a categorical variable, or should we treat it as a scale variable instead?








TipSolution






Levels: 11 valid categories, from 0 (“You can’t be too careful”) to 10 (“Most people can be trusted”), exactly as on the ESS showcard. The questionnaire also has codes for “Refusal” (77) and “Don’t know” (88), which the dataset already defines as missing.
Missing values: 4 of the 1,684 respondents (1 refusal and 3 “Don’t know”), leaving 1,680 valid answers.
Mode: 7, chosen by 339 respondents (20.2% of valid answers). The mode is simply the most common answer.
“Most people can be trusted” (10): only 31 respondents, 1.8%. Very few people choose the extreme of the scale.
What the distribution tells us: answers cluster in the middle and upper-middle of the scale (5 and 7 are the two most common answers). Just over half of respondents (51.7%) answered 6 or higher, and 48.3% answered 5 or lower. The British public leans slightly towards trust, but rarely without reservation.
Categorical or scale? Strictly, the 11 answers are ordered categories (an ordinal variable): we don’t know that the step from 2 to 3 means the same as the step from 7 to 8. In practice, rating scales this long are usually treated as scale variables, which lets us use the mean and standard deviation. Either choice is defensible if you make it consciously and say so.







You may have answered to the last question point that our “social trust” variable (ppltrst) should instead be treated as a “Scale” variable, because it measures its concept on a relatively “long” discrete ordinal scale running from 0 to 10. If so, then we can change the type of the variable to “Scale” so that JASP recognises it as such in statistical analyses.
Step 1: Begin a new analysis in the same JASP workbook and it will be added to our current work; let’s click again on the Descriptives > Descriptive Statistics menu option and start a new descriptive analysis;
Step 2: Let’s move the “social trust” variable again into the Variables field;
Step 3: But now let’s click on the measurement type icon, which will bring up the options we see in the image below:





Change the measurement type to “Scale” and check how the Descriptive Statistics output table on the right hand side has changed. Now that the variable is recognised as a numeric scale measure, we are shown the full set of relevant statistics: Minimum and Maximum values, the Mean, and the Standard Deviation.



We can select many additional descriptive statistic if we want to by clicking on the Statistics option:





Check the Mode and the Median boxes too and look at how the output table has changed. Think about the questions below.

Questions

What is the average level of social trust in this sample?
What is the median level of trust in this sample? Comparing the median to the mean, what can we say about the distribution of our social trust variable?
What is the most common answer category?
Is this “social trust” variable a categorical variable, or should we treat it as a scale variable instead?








TipSolution








Statistic
ppltrst (treated as Scale)




Valid
1,680


Missing
4


Mean
5.40


Median
6


Mode
7


Standard deviation
2.30


Minimum
0


Maximum
10




Average: the mean level of trust is 5.40 on the 0-10 scale.
Median vs mean: the median (6) is higher than the mean (5.40). A tail of very low answers (0 to 2, chosen by 13% of respondents) pulls the mean down, while more people answer above the middle of the scale than below it. The distribution is mildly left-skewed (skewed towards low values).
Most common answer: 7.
Categorical or scale? See the solution to Task 4. Notice that treating the variable as Scale gives us the mean and standard deviation, which only make sense if we accept that the steps between answers are roughly equal.







Start a new descriptive analysis in this same JASP file and describe the age and the sex variable, just like we have done with “social trust”.






TipSolution






















Age (agea, Scale): 1,647 valid answers; 37 respondents have no age recorded (code 999, “Not available”, already set as missing). Ages run from 15 to 90 (the ESS samples people aged 15 and over). Mean 53.6 years, median 54, standard deviation 19.0.
Sex (gndr, Nominal): 824 men (48.9%) and 860 women (51.1%), with no missing values. For a nominal variable the mean and standard deviation are meaningless: report counts and percentages.






To save your analysis, click through Hamburger menu tab > Save as > Computer > Browse and save the analysis in your data folder with the name “ess11-example.jasp” (or anything else that you find useful). Once it’s saved, you can close the analysis. You can now open the .jasp file you saved and continue or modify the analysis you have started.
Once your analysis is saved, you can close this JASP session.




About 30 minutes
Now open a new JASP session and import another of the downloaded datasets. Perform a univariate descriptive analysis of the variables related to social trust and other variables in the dataset similar to what you have done above. When complete, save that analysis to a .jasp file too.
To practice, explore a few of the downloaded datasets. The lecture showed how each survey asked the trust question; for each dataset you open:

Find the trust variable (ISSP_Q25, ISSP_Q36, SocTrust, PeopTrs3, PTrust or STrustGen2B) and request a frequency table.
Compare the values in the table with their labels. Which answers are substantive, and which are non-answers (“Don’t know”, “Can’t choose”, “Refusal”, “Prefer not to answer”)? Are the non-answers already counted as Missing, or are they treated as valid?
Decide whether the variable should be treated as Nominal, Ordinal or Scale, and request the statistics that make sense for that type.







WarningCheck the codes, not just the labels



Survey files often store non-answers as ordinary values (for example 8 = “Don’t know”, 12 = “Can’t choose”). Unless the dataset defines them as missing, JASP treats them as valid answers: they will appear in the frequency table, and they will distort any mean you calculate. We learn how to set them as missing in Workshop 4. Also check how 0-10 scales are stored: in some datasets the answer “0” is stored as the value 1, “1” as 2, and so on.



Questions

Which non-answer codes would you need to set as missing in each dataset?
For which datasets could you meaningfully calculate a mean? What would you need to watch out for?
Using the substantive answers only, what share of respondents gives a “trusting” answer in each survey? Why do the surveys disagree so much?








TipSolution





All figures use the full datasets as downloaded.

Citizenship Survey 2010-11, PTrust

A mean makes sense for the two 0-10 scales and, arguably, the 1-5 scale, but only after setting the non-answers as missing. Otherwise “Can’t choose” (12) and “Prefer not to answer” (99) are averaged in as if they were very high levels of trust. Remember also that the 0-10 answers are stored one value too high: JASP’s mean for ISSP_Q25 will be 5.31 (and 7.05 for STrustGen2B), which is 4.31 (and 6.05) on the scale respondents actually saw.
Why the surveys disagree: between about a third and a half of respondents give a trusting answer, and the two 0-10 scales give means almost two points apart. The questions differ in wording (“can be trusted” vs “how much do you trust”), answer options (forced choice, a middle category, an unoffered “depends”), how they were administered (interview, self-completion, online), and who was sampled (Britain, or England and Wales, or England only). The level of trust is partly a product of how we measure it, which is why comparisons across surveys must be made with great care.







Below are some research questions that you can choose from to address in Assignment 1:

Are religious people more satisfied with life?
Are older people more likely to see the death penalty as justifiable?
What factors are associated with opinions about future European Union enlargement among Europeans?
Is higher internet use associated with stronger anti-immigrant sentiments?
How does victimisation relate to trust in the police?
What factors are associated with belief in life after death?
Are government/public sector employees more inclined to perceive higher levels of corruption than those working in the private sector?

For now, choose one question that you find most sympathetic (you don’t need to stick with it for the assignment, but you could if you wanted to!). All of the questions can be answered with at least one of the survey datasets available on the Data page under the “Assessment Data” heading, and often more than one dataset contains potentially relevant variables.

Identify your “explanandum” - i.e. the core phenomenon/concept/behaviour/etc. that the research question aims to explain. The questions all postulate a relationship/association between two or more variables (the topic of the next workshop), but for now, think carefully about the question and how it is formulated, and identify which is the variable that will be the target of explanation, and which variable (if mentioned) will be used for explaining it. For example, in the research question “Does education increase social trust?”, the variable we are interested in explaining is “social trust”, while “education” is the variable that we will use to explain it. In later workshops we will develop better vocabulary to describe associations between variables.
Once the core phenomenon to be explained is identified, look through the two survey questionnaires to identify any variables that might exist in the dataset that captures it. This may require some trial-and-error with testing out search words.
Once you have found one (or several) candidate variable(s), navigate to the relevant survey website and select a single country for which to download data. You will be working with single-country datasets for your assignment. Download the dataset, import it into JASP, find the relevant variable and perform some descriptive analysis on the chosen variable as you have done in the previous exercise.
Make sure to add your noted and interpretations on the analysis results and save your analysis for later. You could create a new sub-folder for your “Assignment 1” work and save your analysis there for future use. If you end up liking your chosen question, you can continue this analysis in the next workshop.







Navigate to the The World Values Survey (WVS) website and read about the World Values Survey.


Don’t spend too much time browsing the website, but make sure you can answer the following questions:

When was the WVS started, and how many waves of data collection have there been so far?
In which year(s) did the most recent wave of data collection take place?
How many countries were covered by the most recent wave?
Can you name some of the topics covered by the WVS?
What population are the national samples representative of?
What is the general minimum sample size per country?
Is the WVS data freely available for academic research purposes?
Do you need to cite/reference the WVS data if you use it in your research?
Bonus: what is the difference between a time series dataset and a panel dataset, and which of the two can the WVS provide? (tip: look under Data and Documentation > Data Download > Timeseries (1981-2022) for a concise discussion)



Navigate to Data and Documentation > Data Download > Wave 7 (2017-2022) page and explore the Questionnaire and Documentation. Download the Master Questionnaire and the Codebook documents and using the search function identify all the survey questions and variables that relate to “trust”.


Questions

How many questions relating to trust have you identified in the questionnaires?
What is the difference between the questionnaire and the codebook?
In how many different ways is trust measured in the WVS?
What are, in your opinion, the advantages and disadvantages of the different measurements of trust?



Within the “Data” sub-folder you created earlier, create another sub-folder called “WVS7”. You can now save the Master Questionnaire and the Codebook into that folder, and because it is stored on the institutional OneDrive, you will always have access to it on any computer, once you log in to your institutional Microsoft Windows account.
In the Select a country panel on the right side of the Wave 7 (2017-2022) page select one country at random and under Data files download the country-specific dataset (for consistency, download the first data type option, CSV (i.e. comma separated values)) to the “WVS7” subfolder you created earlier.




About 20 minutes
Let’s now navigate to The European Social Survey (ESS) and read about the survey. Try to answer to yourself the same questions as in the previous exercise

Navigate to Data and then to the ESS Data Portal > ESS Round 10 - 2020 > ESS10 - Study Documentation. Download the ESS10 Source questionnaires to a newly created sub-folder called “ESS10”, and as in the previous exercise, identify all the survey questions and variables that relate to “trust”.
Navigate to ESS Data Portal > Datafile Builder (Wizard) and select one country at random at Round 10 (or 10SC). Keep all the variables (do not select any subsets in the “Select Variables” tab) and download the country-specific dataset in CSV format to your “ESS10” folder.

To be able to download data, you will need to register for free with the European Social Survey. Once registered, you have access to a large amount of sociological data at your fingertips.

How many levels (categories) does the variable have in your dataset? Is it what you had expected based on the questionnaire information from the lecture slides?
Does the variable have any missing values in your dataset?
What is the “Mode” of the variable, and what does that mean?
What percentage of the respondents in your dataset had answered that “Most people can be trusted”?
What is the most common answer category, and what do these descriptive statistics tell you about social trust in this sample?
Is this “social trust” variable a categorical variable, or should we treat it as a scale variable instead?








TipSolution






Levels: 11 valid categories, from 0 (“You can’t be too careful”) to 10 (“Most people can be trusted”), exactly as on the ESS showcard. The questionnaire also has codes for “Refusal” (77) and “Don’t know” (88), which the dataset already defines as missing.
Missing values: 4 of the 1,684 respondents (1 refusal and 3 “Don’t know”), leaving 1,680 valid answers.
Mode: 7, chosen by 339 respondents (20.2% of valid answers). The mode is simply the most common answer.
“Most people can be trusted” (10): only 31 respondents, 1.8%. Very few people choose the extreme of the scale.
What the distribution tells us: answers cluster in the middle and upper-middle of the scale (5 and 7 are the two most common answers). Just over half of respondents (51.7%) answered 6 or higher, and 48.3% answered 5 or lower. The British public leans slightly towards trust, but rarely without reservation.
Categorical or scale? Strictly, the 11 answers are ordered categories (an ordinal variable): we don’t know that the step from 2 to 3 means the same as the step from 7 to 8. In practice, rating scales this long are usually treated as scale variables, which lets us use the mean and standard deviation. Either choice is defensible if you make it consciously and say so.







You may have answered to the last question point that our “social trust” variable (ppltrst) should instead be treated as a “Scale” variable, because it measures its concept on a relatively “long” discrete ordinal scale running from 0 to 10. We can select many additional descriptive statistic if we want to by clicking on the Statistics option:

About 30 minutes

To practice, explore a few of the downloaded datasets. The lecture showed how each survey asked the trust question; for each dataset you open:
