Nagelkerke R2 = 0.019 (age-only model: 0.004).

Age barely changes (0.0059 → 0.0062), so adding sex hardly alters what we learn about age. That is what we would expect if age and sex are only weakly related to each other in the sample.
Sex: among respondents of the same age, women’s odds of saying “most people can be trusted” are about 35% lower than men’s (OR = 0.646, because \((0.646 - 1) \times 100 = -35.4\%\)).
In probabilities: the model predicts that a man aged 40 has a 49.8% probability of trusting, and a woman aged 40 has 39.1%: a gap of about 11 percentage points. Notice that “35% lower odds” and “11 points lower probability” describe the same result; only the second is easy for a general reader to picture.
Fit improves from 0.004 to 0.019, but remains very small: age and sex together explain only a sliver of the variation in social trust.










TipTip: odds ratios in JASP



The Odds Ratio column comes from Statistics > Odds ratios, which is ticked by default: you never need to exponentiate by hand. If you also tick Confidence intervals, JASP shows them on the odds-ratio scale by default (we will use these in Workshop 5).








TipTip: plot logistic coefficients on a probability scale



One useful reporting trick - especially when we also have categorical/indicator predictors - is to plot the coefficients on a probability scale. If you recall, this means that we re-convert the “log-odds” and the “odds ratio” coefficients to probabilities, which has some nice properties - it runs from \(0-1\), just like proportions - allowing for easier interpretations.
We can do that by requesting [Inferential plots >] Conditional estimates plots under the plots drop-down option set, which will result in the following output:










JASP Analysis panel











JASP Results panel






Logistic regression: Conditional estimates plots















Important



To model this variable, we need to recode the values of PeopTrs3 manually so it only has 0 and 1 values. That means that we need to make a decision on how to group together the individual values of the \(1\ldots5\) valid scale on which the variable was measured. We could recode all values from \(1-3\) into \(0\) and \(4-5\) into \(1\), or could have \(1-2\) as \(0\) and \(3-5\) as \(1\). Run some univariate descriptive statistics and some bivariate visualisations to check the empirical distribution of the variable; think about the logic underpinning the variable and survey question; then you can make a decision that you can defend.
In practical data analysis you will often encounter situations when you will want to recode categorical variables into fewer categories than the original scale. Such a situation may emerge in the course of an assignment task in which the variable chosen as dependent variable in a planned regression model is multi-categorical (multinomial). There are special statistical models for such dependent variables, however, in this module we are not covering these more advanced methods. Instead, you will want to transform the variables - if logically, conceptually or theoretically possible - into binary/binomial/dichotomous variables (i.e. variables with only two categories).
Such transformations are easy to implement in JASP, and the procedure amounts to manually re-coding the values of the categories by giving several categories the same values. I demonstrate how to recode multinomial variables in the two videos below:


To follow the example transformations in the demo videos, you can use the data_transformation dataset available to download from the module website’s Data page.




Continue in the same JASP file. PeopTrs3 was only asked of respondents to questionnaire version A, in the self-completion booklet, so start by checking how many valid answers it has compared with SocTrust (asked in version C).



Request a frequency table for PeopTrs3 (remember to raise the Maximum distinct values if needed).

Questions

Which values are substantive answers, and which should be treated as missing?
Where is the most common answer on the 1-5 scale?
Look back at Figure 1 (b): only the two ends of the scale have word labels. What might a “3” mean to a respondent?








TipSolution





Values 1 (“You can’t be too careful”) to 5 (“Most people can be trusted”) are substantive; 8 (“Can’t choose”, n = 20) and 9 (“Not answered”, n = 15) should be set as missing. The codes −2 and −1 (versions B and C, and respondents who did not return the self-completion booklet) are already defined as missing in the file. That leaves 892 valid answers:

The middle value, 3, is the most common answer. Because the middle has no label, a “3” could mean genuine ambivalence, “it depends on who”, or simply a cautious non-committal answer.







Set 8 and 9 as missing values (the same way you did for SocTrust).
Create a dichotomous version of the variable with 1 = trusting and 0 = not trusting. You will need to decide where the middle value 3 belongs: with the trusting answers (3-5 = 1) or with the distrusting ones (4-5 = 1, 1-3 = 0)? Use the two videos above to recode the values.
Check the result with a new frequency table: you should have only two categories, with “trusting” coded as 1.







Important



There is no single right answer to where the cut goes, but there are better and worse justifications. Write down your reason before you look at any regression results, so that the results can’t influence the choice.





Create contingency tables of your new dichotomous variable by Sex and by AgeCat (column percentages), as you did for SocTrust.



Fit a logistic regression of your dichotomous PeopTrs3 variable on Age alone, then interpret the odds ratio for Age.



Add Sex to the model (as a Factor). Then repeat Tasks 3-6 with the other cut-point, so that you have two versions of the same model.




Questions

With your preferred cut-point, how are age and sex associated with trust?
Do your conclusions change when you use the other cut-point? Which coefficients change, and how much?
Compare the proportion “trusting” from PeopTrs3 with the 45.4% from SocTrust. Respondents were randomly allocated to questionnaire versions, so the two groups should be comparable. What does the comparison tell you about measuring social trust?








TipSolution





The proportion “trusting” depends heavily on the cut: 39.6% with 4-5 = 1, and 67.8% with 3-5 = 1.
Model results (n = 892, Sex reference = Male):

The conclusions flip. With option A, older respondents have higher odds of trusting (about 1.1% higher odds per year, or 11% per decade) and the sex difference is not statistically significant. With option B, age shows no clear association, while women have about 26% lower odds of trusting than men of the same age.
Why? Moving the “3”s changes who counts as trusting. Under option A, the 3s are grouped with distrust, so the model contrasts confident trusters (4-5) with everyone else; under option B, it contrasts confident distrusters (1-2) with everyone else. Women are more likely than men to choose the most distrustful answer (23.7% vs 15.4% chose “1”), which is why the sex difference appears when the contrast is at the bottom end of the scale.
What to do in practice: choose the cut that best matches your concept and research question, say so explicitly, and report how sensitive your results are to a reasonable alternative. If the substantive conclusion changes, that is itself a finding worth reporting.
Measurement: the binary SocTrust question (45.4% trusting) sits between the two dichotomised versions of the five-point question (39.6% and 67.8%). The same concept, asked of comparable random subsamples of the same survey, produces quite different “levels” of trust depending on the question format. Comparisons of trust levels across surveys that use different question formats should therefore be treated with great caution.














Caution Exercise 4.1.2. Dataset



Download the gb-cs10-trust.sav dataset and open it in JASP. The dataset is also available on the Data page.








Figure 11: Social Trust operationalised in the 2010-2011 Citizenship Survey



The Citizenship Survey measured social trust in a slightly different way, and with a much larger sample. Two things to know about the data before you start:

Coverage: the 2010-11 survey sampled adults aged 16 and over in England and Wales (not Scotland), so strictly it can speak to “Britain” only partially.
Design: alongside the main sample, it included an ethnic minority boost of about 5,000 interviews. Our reduced dataset has no survey weights, so ethnic minority respondents are over-represented in unweighted analyses. Keep this in mind as a limitation.



Identify the trust, age and sex variables (PTrust, xRage or Ragecat, rsex) and summarise them. Check that xRage is set to Scale.




Questions

How many answer categories does PTrust have? Which one did interviewers not read out?
What share of respondents gave that answer?








TipSolution





PTrust has three substantive categories (percentages of the 16,926 valid answers): “People can be trusted” (36.9%), “You can’t be too careful” (50.6%), and a volunteered “Depends” (12.6%), which interviewers recorded when respondents refused the either/or choice. “Don’t know” (40 cases) is already defined as missing.






The key decision is what to do with “Depends”. Two defensible options:

Option 1: set “Depends” as missing, keeping the same either/or contrast as the BSA question.
Option 2: code “Depends” as 0 (not trusting), on the logic that someone who will not say “most people can be trusted” does not hold generalised trust.

Then make sure “People can be trusted” is the category coded 1 (reverse the label order or recode, as you did for SocTrust).



Cross-tabulate your outcome by rsex and by Ragecat (column percentages).



Fit a logistic regression of the outcome on xRage.



Add rsex as a Factor. Fit the model once for each way of handling “Depends”.




Questions

Compare these results with the 2010 BSA (SocTrust) model. What is similar, and what is different? Why might the age coefficient be statistically significant here but not in the BSA?

Age: each additional year is associated with about 1.1% higher odds of trusting (around 12% per decade), holding sex constant. With “Depends” set as missing, the share trusting rises from about a third of 16-24-year-olds (34%) to almost half of those aged 75+ (49%).

“Depends” barely matters here: both coefficients move only slightly. That robustness is worth reporting.
Compared with the BSA 2010: the direction of both associations is the same (older people more trusting; women less trusting). The sex difference is smaller in the Citizenship Survey (OR 0.82 vs 0.65). The age coefficient is larger (1.011 vs 1.006) and, with 14 times as many respondents, it is estimated far more precisely, which is why it is clearly statistically significant here. Remember also that the samples differ in coverage (England and Wales vs Britain), age range (16+ vs mainly 18+) and design (ethnic minority boost, no weights).

title: Workshop 4 Worksheet
text:
You will use the following three datasets, in turn, to model social phenomena in “post-pandemic” Britain:

Community Life Survey 2023-24 (gb-cls23-trust_nm.sav)
British Social Attitudes Survey 2023 (gb-bsa23-trust.sav)
British Social Attitudes Survey 2024 (gb-bsa24-trust.sav)







ImportantRead the question closely




“Young people (under-24s)”: none of the datasets lets us isolate exactly the under-24s. The youngest age group available is 16-24 (CLS and BSA 2024) or 18-24 (BSA 2023). Use that group, and say so explicitly in your write-up.
“Lower social trust”: lower than whom? The natural comparison is everyone aged 25 and over. You will therefore need to collapse the age groups into a two-category variable (young vs older).
“Post-pandemic Britain”: the CLS covers England only, while the BSA covers Great Britain. And a single post-pandemic survey cannot tell us whether young people’s trust is lower than it used to be: for that we would need a pre-pandemic comparison (you have one in Exercise 4.1.2!).











Caution Exercise 4.2.1 Dataset



Download the gb-cls23-trust_nm.sav dataset and open it in JASP. The dataset is also available on the Data page.








Figure 12: “Social trust” operationalised in the 2023-2024 Community Life Survey



Read the research question carefully and identify what it does and doesn’t tell you about the variables, data selection and modelling methods that are needed to address the question as directly as possible. Consider the following questions in particular:

Which “age” variable would you choose if you had more than one option available, and what kind of transformation may be useful in order to answer your research question?
Do you need to transform your outcome/dependent variable, or can it be modelled as it is? (You may have different option here!)
If you wanted to fit a binary logistic regression model, how would you need to transform the outcome variable, if at all?
Can you fit two different types of regression models and compare the results?
Do you have any other eligible “control” variables at your disposal in the dataset? If so, what would be the benefit of including them in the model?



The dataset has three variables of interest: STrustGen2B (trust in most people), Ragecat (age in seven groups) and Sex. There is no numeric age variable, so the age groups are all we have.






WarningCheck the codes, not just the labels



The 0-10 trust answers are stored as the values 1 to 11 (the value 1 carries the label “0. Not at all”, the value 11 the label “10. Completely”). If you treat the variable as Scale, JASP uses the stored values, so every mean and intercept will be one point higher than on the 0-10 scale respondents saw. Differences between groups, and therefore regression coefficients, are not affected.





Request frequency tables for all three variables, and descriptive statistics for STrustGen2B treated as Scale.

Questions

Which values of Sex and Ragecat should not count as valid answers? Are they already set as missing?
What is the most common answer on the trust scale, and what is the mean (on the 0-10 scale)?






Sex: set “Prefer not to say” (−9) as missing. (It is not one of the missing values defined in the file.)
Ragecat: check that “Item not applicable” (−1) is missing, then create a two-category version: 16-24 (16-19 and 20-24) vs 25+ (all other groups). Code 25+ as the first category, so that it becomes the reference group in regression models.
STrustGen2B: you have two options, and this exercise asks you to try both:

keep it as an 11-point Scale variable and use linear regression; or
dichotomise it for logistic regression. A natural cut is above the scale’s midpoint: 6-10 = 1 (trusting) and 0-5 = 0. (Remember: in the stored values that is 7-11 vs 1-6.)





Use Descriptives > Descriptive Statistics with trust in Variables (as Scale) and the seven age groups in Split, and add box plots. Then do the same with your two-group age variable.



Fit (a) a linear regression of the 0-10 trust scale on the young/older variable, and (b) a logistic regression of the dichotomised trust variable on the same predictor.



Add Sex (as a Factor) to both models.




Questions

By how much does trust differ between 16-24-year-olds and those aged 25+, on the 0-10 scale and in terms of odds?
Does adjusting for sex change the answer?
Look back at the seven age groups: are 16-24-year-olds distinctive, or part of a wider age pattern?








TipSolution





After setting the missing values, 50,706 respondents have valid answers on all three variables (5,040 aged 16-24).

Descriptives: the mean trust score is 6.07 on the 0-10 scale (7.07 in the stored values) and the most common answer is 7. Mean trust is 5.54 among 16-24-year-olds and 6.13 among those aged 25+.
Linear model (young + sex): 16-24-year-olds score 0.59 points lower on the 0-10 scale than those aged 25+ (95% CI −0.65 to −0.53, p < .001). Sex (Male): −0.01, p = .46. R2 = 0.007.
Logistic model (6-10 = trusting): 54.5% of 16-24-year-olds vs 66.4% of those aged 25+ are “trusting”. The odds ratio for the young group is 0.60 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.64, p < .001): their odds of trusting are about 40% lower. Sex (Male): OR 0.99, p = .75.
Adjusting for sex changes nothing, because trust barely differs by sex in this survey.
The wider age pattern matters for interpretation. Mean trust by age group:

20-24

5.64
5.45

25-34-year-olds trust as little as 16-24-year-olds; after that, trust rises steadily with age. So the answer is “yes, young adults report lower trust”, but the young are not uniquely low: the comparison with all those aged 25+ mixes in a long age gradient. A single cross-section also cannot tell us whether this is an age effect (people become more trusting as they get older), a cohort effect (younger generations are less trusting), or a period effect of the pandemic.













Caution Exercise 4.2.2 Dataset



Download the gb-bsa23-trust.sav dataset and open it in JASP. The dataset is also available on the Data page.


The “social trust” variable in this dataset poses similar (but somewhat simpler) data transformation challenges to those encountered with the 2010 BSA (Self-completion) “social trust” variable.






Figure 13: “Social trust” operationalised in the 2023 BSA





The variables of interest are ISSP_Q36 (trust), Ragecat (age in eight groups), RespAge_Archive (age in years) and DVsex23 (sex). Note that ISSP_Q36 was only asked in some questionnaire versions, so most rows are “Not applicable” by design.






TipTwo age variables



RespAge_Archive is bottom-coded: everyone aged 18 to 22 is stored as 22, and anyone 80 or older as 80 (a common disclosure-control step in archived survey data). You can still identify the 18-24 group with it (values 22, 23 and 24), but Ragecat (value 1 = “18-24” for the BSA sample) is the more transparent choice.





Request frequency tables for ISSP_Q36, Ragecat and DVsex23, and identify the answers that are not substantive.




ISSP_Q36: set “Can’t choose” (5) and “Prefer not to answer” (9) as missing. Recode “almost always” and “usually” trusted (1, 2) as 1, and the two “can’t be too careful” answers (3, 4) as 0.
Ragecat: set “Don’t know/Refused/Not answered” (9) as missing; recode 18-24 (1) vs 25+ (2-8), with 25+ as the reference category.
DVsex23: set “Prefer not to answer” (9) as missing.




Cross-tabulate the dichotomised trust variable by your two-group age variable (column percentages).



Fit a logistic regression of trust on the young/older variable.



Add DVsex23 as a Factor. Note that in this survey Female is the first category, so JASP will report a coefficient for DVsex23 (Male).




Questions

What are the odds ratio and the predicted proportions trusting for 18-24-year-olds compared with those aged 25+?
How many 18-24-year-olds is this estimate based on? What does that suggest about its precision?








TipSolution





After the transformations, 1,504 respondents have valid answers on all three variables, but only 80 of them are aged 18-24.

33.8% of 18-24-year-olds say people can almost always or usually be trusted, compared with 48.6% of those aged 25+.
Simple model: young OR = 0.54 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.87, p = .011).
Adjusting for sex: young OR = 0.56 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.91, p = .018): the odds of trusting are about 44% lower for 18-24-year-olds than for older respondents of the same sex. DVsex23 (Male): OR = 1.43 (p < .001), so men have about 43% higher odds of trusting than women.
The direction and size of the age difference are similar to the CLS, but with only 80 young respondents the interval is very wide: the true odds ratio could plausibly be anywhere from about 10% lower to about 65% lower.














Caution Exercise 4.2.3 Dataset



Download the gb-bsa24-trust.sav dataset and open it in JASP. The dataset is also available on the Data page.


The “social trust” variable in this dataset is similar to the one encountered in the 2023-2024 Community Life Survey.






Figure 14: “Social trust” operationalised in the 2024 BSA





The variables of interest are ISSP_Q25 (trust, 0-10), Ragecat (age in eight groups) and DVsex24 (sex). As in the CLS, the 0-10 answers are stored as the values 1 to 11.



Request frequency tables and identify the non-substantive answers.




ISSP_Q25: set “Can’t choose” (12) and “Prefer not to answer” (99) as missing. Keep a Scale version for linear regression and create a dichotomous version (6-10 = 1, 0-5 = 0) for logistic regression, exactly as for the CLS.
Ragecat: set code 9 as missing and recode 16-24 (1) vs 25+ (2-8).
DVsex24: set “Prefer not to answer” (9) as missing.




Compare mean trust (as Scale) between the two age groups, and cross-tabulate the dichotomised version by age group.



Fit a linear model (0-10 scale) and a logistic model (dichotomised) with the young/older variable as the only predictor.



Fit both the linear and the logistic model with the young/older variable and DVsex24.




Questions

Is there a statistically significant difference in trust between 16-24-year-olds and those aged 25+ in the BSA 2024?
Does that mean the BSA 2024 contradicts the CLS 2023-24?
Compare the average trust score in the BSA 2024 with the CLS. Both use a 0-10 scale: why might the averages be so different?








TipSolution





1,453 respondents have valid answers on all three variables, of whom only 78 are aged 16-24.

Mean trust: 4.14 (16-24) vs 4.33 (25+) on the 0-10 scale.
Linear model: young −0.16 points (95% CI −0.71 to 0.40, p = .58). DVsex24 (Male): +0.29 (p = .026).
Logistic model (6-10 = trusting): 28.2% vs 31.6% trusting; young OR = 0.87 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.44, p = .58).

The difference is in the same direction as in the CLS but small and not statistically significant. That does not contradict the CLS: the BSA’s confidence interval (−0.71 to 0.40) comfortably includes the CLS estimate of −0.59. With 78 young respondents the BSA 2024 simply cannot estimate the age difference precisely: “no statistically significant difference” is not the same as “no difference” (more on this in Workshop 5).
The averages differ a lot (about 4.3 in the BSA vs 6.1 in the CLS) because the questions differ. The BSA scale runs from “You can’t be too careful” to “Most people can be trusted”; the CLS asks how much you trust most people, from “Not at all” to “Completely”. Different wording, anchors and survey designs put respondents’ answers in different places on the scale, so levels of trust should not be compared across surveys, even when both use 0-10.








Questions

Write a three-sentence answer to the research question “Do young people (under-24s) have lower social trust in post-pandemic Britain?”, using all three surveys.
Look back at Exercise 4.1.2: were young people also the least trusting group in 2010-11? What does that suggest about the “post-pandemic” part of the question?








TipSolution





One possible answer:

Across three recent surveys, young adults (16/18-24) report lower generalised trust than those aged 25 and over: 0.6 points lower on a 0-10 scale in the large Community Life Survey (England, 2023-24), with 40% lower odds of trusting, and 44% lower odds in the British Social Attitudes 2023. The British Social Attitudes 2024 shows a smaller difference that is not statistically significant, but its sample contains only 78 young respondents and its estimate is consistent with the other two. Trust rises steadily with age from the mid-30s, and the same pattern was already visible in the 2010-11 Citizenship Survey, so the evidence does not show that low trust among the young is a specifically post-pandemic phenomenon.

In the 2010-11 Citizenship Survey, about 34% of 16-24-year-olds said most people can be trusted, compared with almost half of those aged 75+. Young people were already the least trusting group a decade before the pandemic: to claim that the pandemic changed young people’s trust, we would need comparable measurements of the same population before and after it.

title: Workshop 4 Worksheet
text:
Let’s look again at the assignment research questions. Some of these questions imply a dependent variable which is measured as a numeric scale or at least a long-ish (e.g. 7-point +) ordinal scale in one of the surveys we will use for the assignment (ESS10, WVS7, EVS2017). Other questions imply dependent variables that are more strictly categorical, and as such, we cannot model them using linear regression. For those, we may be able to apply a logistic regression model.
If your chosen outcome variable is categorical with more than two categories but too few (fewer than about seven) to treat as a scale, you will have to dichotomise it in order to use it as a dependent variable in a logistic regression. While there are specific modelling methods for “multinomial” type outcome variables, we are not covering them on this module.
In this exercise, explore the assignment dataset using the Variable search function on the website to identify any available variables for answering one/some of the questions below, and check how the implied dependent variable was measured:

Are religious people more satisfied with life?
Are older people more likely to see the death penalty as justifiable?
What factors are associated with opinions about future European Union enlargement among Europeans?
Is higher internet use associated with stronger anti-immigrant sentiments?
How does victimisation relate to trust in the police?
What factors are associated with belief in life after death?
Are government/public sector employees more inclined to perceive higher levels of corruption than those working in the private sector?

title: Workshop 4 Worksheet
text:
Read the article by Delhey and Newton (2003) and download the delhey&newton2003.sav dataset from the Data page. The dataset is quite complex and the original variables have not been renamed and labelled, so it is essential to engage with the Original Questionnaire and the Original Codebook in order to understand the data and identify relevant variables. Appendix 1 in Delhey and Newton (2003), pp.115-117 provides more details about the construction of variables from the original survey items.
Read the research question carefully and identify what it does and doesn’t tell you about the variables, data selection and modelling methods that are needed to address the question as directly as possible. Consider the following steps in particular:

Choose two countries to contrast with two separate analyses
Filter the dataset by country and run your separate analyses on these partial samples
In your models, include all three demographic variables used by Delhey and Newton (2003) in their models (gender, age and education) and select three additional explanatory variables as you please, but think carefully about the logic underpinning your choices
Transform any variables as needed (e.g. the education variable needs to be re-coded into three categories - “primary”, “secondary” and “tertiary” - to replicate the coding choices made by the original authors.
Don’t expect your results to necessarily come close to those in the published article based on more complex (too complex?) models, but check your results against the relevant “total” regression results tables (not the Summary tables) presented in Appendix 2 of Delhey and Newton (2003), pp.118-131.

title: Week 5 Self-check Quiz: Uncertainty and inference
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 5 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. The examples use the same data as the lecture and Worksheet 5.


Why do we need confidence intervals and p-values at all?

Because survey data always contain mistakes
Because a different random sample would give a different estimate, and we want to say something about the population
Because JASP requires them
Because the mean is not reliable







TipAnswer





b. Every random sample gives a slightly different answer. Inference describes how far a single sample’s estimate is likely to be from the population value.






What happens to the standard error of a proportion if the sample size is four times larger?

It becomes four times smaller
It becomes about half as large
It stays the same
It becomes larger







TipAnswer





b. The standard error shrinks with the square root of the sample size: √4 = 2.






In the BSA 2010, 45.4% of 1,060 respondents say most people can be trusted (95% CI 42.3% to 48.4%). Which statement is correct?

95% of respondents gave an answer between 42.3% and 48.4%
We can be 95% confident that between 42.3% and 48.4% of British adults in 2010 would say most people can be trusted
The survey is 95% accurate
The true share is exactly 45.4%







TipAnswer





b. The interval gives a range of plausible values for the population share. It covers sampling error only, not problems with wording, non-response or coverage.






In a simulation, 50 random samples each produce a 95% confidence interval. About how many intervals would you expect to contain the true population value?

All 50
About 47 or 48
About 25
It’s impossible to say







TipAnswer





b. Across many samples, 95% of intervals built this way contain the true value (in the lecture’s simulation, 47 of 50). For any single real interval, we cannot know whether it is one of the hits or one of the misses.






An analyst claims that 20% of households are in poverty; your sample of 500 finds 23%. What is the null hypothesis?

The true share is 23%
The true share is 20%
The true share is not 20%
The sample is biased







TipAnswer





b. The null hypothesis is the “devil’s advocate” position: the claim is correct and our 23% differs from it only by chance.






For that poverty example, p = 0.09. What does this mean?

There is a 9% chance that the analyst is right
If the true share were 20%, samples of 500 at least this far from 20% would turn up about 9% of the time
The difference is 9 percentage points
We have proved the analyst is wrong







TipAnswer





b. The p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the null is true. At the conventional 5% level we would not reject the analyst’s claim, but that doesn’t prove it right either.






A regression coefficient has a 95% CI of −10.98 to −3.32. What can you say about its p-value?

It is below .05
It is above .05
It is exactly .05
Nothing: CIs and p-values are unrelated







TipAnswer





a. A 95% confidence interval excludes 0 exactly when the two-sided p-value is below .05. (This is the inequality coefficient in the Spirit Level model: p < .001.)






Men in the ESS score 0.27 points higher than women on the 0-10 trust scale (95% CI 0.05 to 0.49, p = .015; SD about 2.3). Which description is best?

A large and important gender gap
A statistically significant but small difference: about a tenth of a standard deviation
No real difference, because the gap is small
Men are 27% more trusting







TipAnswer





b. Statistical significance is about how surprising the data would be if there were no difference, not about how big the difference is. Always report the size of the difference and its interval.






In the BSA 2024, 16-24-year-olds score 0.16 points lower than older adults (95% CI −0.71 to 0.40, p = .58; only 78 young respondents). The much larger Community Life Survey finds a gap of −0.59. What should you conclude?

The BSA 2024 shows that young people’s trust is no different
The BSA 2024 is too imprecise to settle the question; its interval includes both 0 and −0.59
The two surveys contradict each other
The Community Life Survey must be wrong







TipAnswer





b. “Not statistically significant” means “not enough evidence”, not “no difference”. The BSA 2024 interval is compatible with no difference and with the CLS estimate.






In a logistic regression, the odds ratio for women is 0.65 with a 95% CI of 0.51 to 0.83. What does the interval tell you?

Women’s odds of trusting are lower than men’s, and the data are not compatible with no difference
The result is not statistically significant because the interval is wide
Women’s probability of trusting is between 51% and 83%
The interval should be checked against 0







TipAnswer





a. For odds ratios, “no difference” is 1, not 0. The whole interval lies below 1, so p < .05. The values are odds ratios, not probabilities.

title: Week 3 Self-check Quiz: Modelling continuous outcomes
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 3 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. Most examples use the Spirit Level data (pickett2009) from the lecture and Worksheet 3: trust is the percentage of people who say most people can be trusted; income inequality is the ratio of the income of the richest fifth to that of the poorest fifth.


The regression of trust on income inequality gives: predicted trust = 77.06 − 6.54 × inequality. What does −6.54 mean?

Trust falls by 6.54% in every country
Countries whose inequality ratio is one unit higher have, on average, 6.54 percentage points lower trust
Inequality explains 6.54% of trust
The correlation between inequality and trust is −6.54







TipAnswer





b. The slope is the average difference in the outcome per one-unit difference in the predictor, in the outcome’s own units.






What does the intercept, 77.06, describe here?

The average trust across the 23 countries
The predicted trust in a country with an inequality ratio of 0, which is impossible, so we don’t interpret it
The maximum possible trust
The trust of the most equal country







TipAnswer





b. The ratio can’t be below 1, so 0 lies far outside the data. The intercept is needed to draw the line but has no substantive meaning here. (The average trust, 38.8%, is the intercept of the null model M₀.)






Using predicted trust = 77.06 − 6.535 × inequality, what is the predicted trust for Portugal (inequality = 8)?

10.0%
24.8%
38.8%
52.3%







TipAnswer





b. 77.06 − 6.535 × 8 = 24.8%. Portugal’s observed trust is 10.0%, so its residual is 10.0 − 24.8 = −14.8 points.






What is a residual?

The part of the outcome explained by the predictor
The observed value minus the value predicted by the line
The slope of the line
A country with missing data







TipAnswer





b. Residuals are what the line gets wrong for each case. Least squares chooses the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible.






The model has R² = 0.44. What does this mean?

The slope is 0.44
Inequality accounts for 44% of the variation in trust across these countries
44% of countries are correctly predicted
Inequality causes 44% of a country’s trust







TipAnswer





b. R² is the share of the variation in the outcome that the model accounts for. The other 56% goes with other things. With one predictor, R² = r² (here (−0.664)² = 0.441).






In a model with both predictors, the coefficient for inequality is −7.15 and for homicides (per million) +0.17. Which conclusion is correct?

Inequality is 40 times more important than homicides
The coefficients are in different units, so their sizes can’t be compared directly; standardized coefficients or R² are needed
Homicides increase trust
Both predictors are equally important







TipAnswer





b. One unit of the inequality ratio and one homicide per million people are not comparable units. Standardized coefficients express both in standard deviations. (And c is wrong twice: the homicide coefficient is tiny and uncertain, and “increase” is causal language.)






What does “adjusting for homicide rates” mean for the inequality coefficient in a multiple regression?

Homicides were removed from the data
The coefficient describes the association between inequality and trust among countries with the same homicide rate
We have proved that homicides don’t affect trust
We ran an experiment that held homicides fixed







TipAnswer





b. Multiple regression compares like with like statistically. It is not an experiment, and it only adjusts for the variables actually in the model.






In a regression of trust on world region with Western Europe as the reference category, the intercept is 40.66 and the coefficient for Asia is −13.96. What is the predicted trust for an Asian country?

−13.96%
13.96%
26.70%
54.62%







TipAnswer





c. 40.66 − 13.96 = 26.70%, which is simply the mean of the Asian countries. Each region’s coefficient is its difference from the reference category.






Protestant countries have mean trust of 48.26% and other countries 24.81%. In a regression of trust on Protestantism (coded 1 = Protestant, 0 = not), what is the coefficient?

24.81
48.26
23.45
0.36







TipAnswer





c. With a single 0/1 predictor, the coefficient is the difference between the two group means (48.26 − 24.81). The intercept (24.81) is the mean of the group coded 0.






Which of these is not a good reason to doubt a regression line?

The scatter plot shows a curved pattern
One extreme case tilts the line
Two predictors are almost perfectly correlated (high VIF)
The R² is below 0.5







TipAnswer





d. A modest R² is normal in social science and does not make the line wrong: it just means other factors matter too. Curvature (Anscombe’s quartet), influential cases and multicollinearity are genuine reasons for caution.

title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 1 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. The examples use the same data as the lecture and Worksheet 1 (mainly the UK sample of the European Social Survey 2023-24, gb-ess11-trust.sav).


Which level of measurement is age in years (agea)?

Nominal
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio







TipAnswer





d. Age has equal steps between values and a true zero, so ratios make sense (a 60-year-old is twice as old as a 30-year-old). In JASP, interval and ratio variables are both treated as Scale.






Which summary makes sense for a nominal variable such as sex (gndr)?

The mean
The median
The mode and the percentage in each category
The standard deviation







TipAnswer





c. Nominal categories have no order, so only counts, percentages and the mode are meaningful. JASP will happily calculate a “mean” of the codes 1 and 2, but it means nothing.






For trust in the ESS (0-10), the mean is 5.40, the median 6 and the mode 7. What does this pattern suggest?

The distribution is perfectly symmetric
A tail of low scores pulls the mean below the median (mild left skew)
A few very high scores pull the mean up (right skew)
The data contain errors







TipAnswer





b. More people answer above the middle of the scale than below, but a tail of very low answers (0 to 2, chosen by 13% of respondents) drags the mean down. In a right-skewed distribution such as income, it’s the other way round: the mean is above the median.






Nine households have incomes (in £000s) of 18, 22, 25, 28, 31, 34, 38, 45 and 400. Which figure best describes a “typical” household?

The mean, 71
The median, 31
The range, 382
The maximum, 400







TipAnswer





b. The single very high income pulls the mean (71) above eight of the nine households. The median (31) is barely affected, which is why incomes and wealth are usually reported as medians.






In the BSA 2010, 484 respondents said “most people can be trusted”, out of 3,297 people in the file. Only 1,081 were asked the question, and 17 of them answered “Don’t know” or refused. Which percentage best describes the share of trusting answers?

484 / 3,297 = 14.7%
484 / 1,081 = 44.8%
484 / 1,064 = 45.5%
All three are equally good







TipAnswer





c. The question was only asked in one version of the questionnaire, so the 2,216 people never asked must be left out of the denominator. “Don’t know” and refusals are not substantive answers either, so the clearest figure uses the 1,064 substantive answers. Always check what the denominator of a percentage is.






In the BSA 2010, 484 respondents said “most people can be trusted” and 580 said “you can’t be too careful”. What is the ratio of trusting to careful answers?

0.45
0.83
1.20
45.5%







TipAnswer





b. 484 ÷ 580 = 0.83: about 8 trusting answers for every 10 careful ones. (0.45 is the proportion trusting, and 1.20 is the ratio the other way round.) In Week 4 this ratio reappears as the odds of trusting.






The standard deviation of trust in the ESS is 2.30. What does it describe?

The typical respondent’s trust score
The typical distance of an answer from the mean
The difference between the highest and lowest answers
The share of respondents within one point of the mean







TipAnswer





b. A typical answer lies about 2.3 points above or below the mean of 5.4. The difference between the highest and lowest answers is the range (here 10).






In a box plot of ESS trust, the box runs from 4 to 7 and the line inside it is at 6. What do these numbers show?

The minimum, maximum and mean
The 25th percentile, the 75th percentile and the median
The mean ± one standard deviation
The two most common answers and the average







TipAnswer





b. The box covers the middle 50% of respondents (the interquartile range, 7 − 4 = 3), and the line marks the median.






Six British surveys asked about trust in “most people”. Depending on the survey, the share giving a trusting answer ranged from about 37% to 48% (11 percentage points apart), and two 0-10 scales had means of 4.3 and 6.1. What is the main lesson?

Trust changed dramatically between surveys
One of the surveys must have made an error
Question wording, answer options and survey design shape the measured level of trust
Social trust cannot be measured







TipAnswer





c. The surveys word the question differently, offer different answer options (two options, a middle category, an unoffered “depends”, 0-10 scales with different labels), use different modes and cover different populations. Levels of trust should only be compared across surveys with great care; comparisons within one survey are much safer.






In the BSA 2024 file, the 0-10 trust question has the extra values 12 (“Can’t choose”) and 99 (“Prefer not to answer”), which are not defined as missing. What happens if you calculate the mean straight away?

Nothing: JASP ignores non-answers automatically
The mean is too high, because 12 and 99 are averaged in as if they were scores
The mean is too low
JASP refuses to calculate a mean







TipAnswer





b. Unless they are set as missing, JASP treats 12 and 99 as valid values and includes them in the mean. Always look at a frequency table, compare values with labels, and set non-answers as missing first (Workshop 4 shows how).

c. Nominal categories have no order, so only counts, percentages and the mode are meaningful. JASP will happily calculate a “mean” of the codes 1 and 2, but it means nothing.

title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
For trust in the ESS (0-10), the mean is 5.40, the median 6 and the mode 7. What does this pattern suggest?

The distribution is perfectly symmetric
A tail of low scores pulls the mean below the median (mild left skew)
A few very high scores pull the mean up (right skew)
The data contain errors







TipAnswer





b. More people answer above the middle of the scale than below, but a tail of very low answers (0 to 2, chosen by 13% of respondents) drags the mean down. In a right-skewed distribution such as income, it’s the other way round: the mean is above the median.

title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
Nine households have incomes (in £000s) of 18, 22, 25, 28, 31, 34, 38, 45 and 400. Which figure best describes a “typical” household?

The mean, 71
The median, 31
The range, 382
The maximum, 400







TipAnswer





b. The single very high income pulls the mean (71) above eight of the nine households. The median (31) is barely affected, which is why incomes and wealth are usually reported as medians.

title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
In the BSA 2010, 484 respondents said “most people can be trusted”, out of 3,297 people in the file. Only 1,081 were asked the question, and 17 of them answered “Don’t know” or refused. Which percentage best describes the share of trusting answers?

484 / 3,297 = 14.7%
484 / 1,081 = 44.8%
484 / 1,064 = 45.5%
All three are equally good







TipAnswer





c. The question was only asked in one version of the questionnaire, so the 2,216 people never asked must be left out of the denominator. “Don’t know” and refusals are not substantive answers either, so the clearest figure uses the 1,064 substantive answers. title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
In the BSA 2010, 484 respondents said “most people can be trusted” and 580 said “you can’t be too careful”. What is the ratio of trusting to careful answers?

0.45
0.83
1.20
45.5%







TipAnswer





b. 484 ÷ 580 = 0.83: about 8 trusting answers for every 10 careful ones. (0.45 is the proportion trusting, and 1.20 is the ratio the other way round.) In Week 4 this ratio reappears as the odds of trusting.

title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
The standard deviation of trust in the ESS is 2.30. What does it describe?

The typical respondent’s trust score
The typical distance of an answer from the mean
The difference between the highest and lowest answers
The share of respondents within one point of the mean







TipAnswer





b. A typical answer lies about 2.3 points above or below the mean of 5.4. The difference between the highest and lowest answers is the range (here 10).

title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
In a box plot of ESS trust, the box runs from 4 to 7 and the line inside it is at 6. What do these numbers show?

The minimum, maximum and mean
The 25th percentile, the 75th percentile and the median
The mean ± one standard deviation
The two most common answers and the average







TipAnswer





b. The box covers the middle 50% of respondents (the interquartile range, 7 − 4 = 3), and the line marks the median.

title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
Six British surveys asked about trust in “most people”. Depending on the survey, the share giving a trusting answer ranged from about 37% to 48% (11 percentage points apart), and two 0-10 scales had means of 4.3 and 6.1. What is the main lesson?

Trust changed dramatically between surveys
One of the surveys must have made an error
Question wording, answer options and survey design shape the measured level of trust
Social trust cannot be measured







TipAnswer





c. The surveys word the question differently, offer different answer options (two options, a middle category, an unoffered “depends”, 0-10 scales with different labels), use different modes and cover different populations. title: Week 1 Self-check Quiz: Measurement and description
text:
In the BSA 2024 file, the 0-10 trust question has the extra values 12 (“Can’t choose”) and 99 (“Prefer not to answer”), which are not defined as missing. What happens if you calculate the mean straight away?

Nothing: JASP ignores non-answers automatically
The mean is too high, because 12 and 99 are averaged in as if they were scores
The mean is too low
JASP refuses to calculate a mean







TipAnswer





b. Unless they are set as missing, JASP treats 12 and 99 as valid values and includes them in the mean. Always look at a frequency table, compare values with labels, and set non-answers as missing first (Workshop 4 shows how).

title: Week 2 Self-check Quiz: Comparisons and associations
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 2 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. The examples use the same data as the lecture and Worksheet 2.


You want to describe how trust on the ESS 0-10 scale differs between men and women. Which tool fits?

A contingency table with row percentages
Group means and medians, shown in box plots
A scatter plot with a correlation
A frequency table of trust







TipAnswer





b. One variable is categorical (sex) and one is treated as scale (trust), so we compare the distribution of trust across the groups. Contingency tables are for two categorical variables; scatter plots for two scale variables.






In a study of age and social trust, which variable is the outcome?

Age
Social trust
Either, it makes no difference
Neither: both are explanatory







TipAnswer





b. Age can plausibly shape trust, but trust cannot change someone’s age. For many pairs (e.g. volunteering and trust) the direction is less obvious, and theory has to decide.






In the BSA 2010, 51.7% of men and 40.7% of women say most people can be trusted. These are column percentages with sex in the columns. What question do they answer?

What share of trusting respondents are men?
Are men or women more likely to say most people can be trusted?
How many respondents trust most people?
Is the difference statistically significant?







TipAnswer





b. Column percentages compare the groups in the columns: men are about 11 percentage points more likely to trust. Row percentages would answer question a (and only describe who the trusting are, which depends on how many men and women were sampled).






Trust is 51.7% among men and 40.7% among women. Which description is correct?

Women are 11% less trusting
Women are 11 percentage points less likely to trust
Women are 21% as trusting as men
The gap is 0.11%







TipAnswer





b. The difference between two percentages is measured in percentage points. In relative terms, 40.7% is about 21% lower than 51.7%, which is a different statement: always say which one you mean.






In the ESS, the box plots of trust for men and women both run from 4 to 7, with medians of 6 (men) and 5 (women). What can you conclude?

Men and women have identical trust
Men trust slightly more on average, but the two distributions overlap almost completely
All men trust more than all women
Women’s trust varies more because their median is lower







TipAnswer





b. The middle 50% of both groups covers the same range; only the medians (and the means, 5.54 vs 5.27) differ slightly. A gap between groups should always be judged against the spread within them.






The correlation between income inequality and trust across 23 rich countries is r = −0.66. What does it mean?

Inequality causes 66% of the variation in trust
More unequal countries tend to have lower trust, and the association is fairly strong
Every unequal country has low trust
66% of countries are unequal







TipAnswer





b. The sign gives the direction (negative: higher inequality, lower trust) and the size gives the strength. There are clear exceptions (e.g. the USA and New Zealand trust more than their inequality would suggest), and a correlation says nothing about cause.






A scatter plot shows a clear U-shaped relationship, yet Pearson’s r is almost exactly 0. Why?

There must be an error in the calculation
r only measures straight-line (linear) association
r is always close to zero for curves with many points
The two variables are unrelated







TipAnswer





b. Pearson’s r captures linear association only. That’s why you should always look at the scatter plot before relying on a correlation.






In the 2024 Spirit Level data (43 countries), the correlation between the income quintile ratio and trust is −0.15, but −0.58 without China. What does this show?

China’s data must be wrong
One unusual case can change a correlation a lot
The 2024 data contradict the 2009 data
The quintile ratio is not a measure of inequality







TipAnswer





b. China combines by far the highest measured inequality with high measured trust, which flattens the line. Look for unusual cases in the scatter plot and report how much they matter.






Unequal countries tend to have lower trust. Can we conclude that poorer individuals trust less?

Yes, that’s what the correlation means
No: country-level data describe countries, not individuals
Yes, if the correlation is strong enough
No, because the correlation is negative







TipAnswer





b. Drawing conclusions about individuals from group-level data is the ecological fallacy. To study individuals we need individual-level survey data.






Which of these explanations for the inequality-trust correlation can the correlation itself rule out?

Inequality erodes trust
Trust reduces inequality (trusting societies support redistribution)
Something else, such as history or institutions, drives both
None of them







TipAnswer





d. A correlation is compatible with all three stories. To weigh them we need theory, other variables (Week 3: multiple regression lets us adjust for some third factors) and ideally data over time.

title: Week 4 Self-check Quiz: Modelling dichotomous outcomes
text:
Ten short questions to check your understanding after the Week 4 lecture. It takes about 10 minutes. Try each question before opening the answer. The examples use the same data as the lecture and Worksheet 4 (British Social Attitudes 2010: SocTrust modelled on age and sex).


Which of these outcome variables calls for logistic rather than linear regression?

Trust in most people, measured on a 0-10 scale (ESS ppltrst)
The percentage of a country’s population who say most people can be trusted
Whether the respondent voted in the last general election (yes/no)
The number of close friends a respondent has







TipAnswer





c. It has only two possible values, so we model the probability of “yes”. The 0-10 scale (a) and the country percentage (b) can be treated as numeric scales; a count (d) is numeric too.






30% of a sample say most people can be trusted. What are the odds of trusting?

0.30
0.43
2.33
0.70







TipAnswer





b. Odds = p ÷ (1 − p) = 0.3 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 0.43, or 3 trusting for every 7 who are not. (2.33 is the odds of not trusting.)






A logistic regression Estimate is 0. What does that mean?

The predicted probability is 0
The odds ratio is 1: the predictor makes no difference to the odds
The predictor perfectly predicts the outcome
Nobody in the sample is in the category coded 1







TipAnswer





b. Estimates are on the log-odds scale, and e⁰ = 1. An odds ratio of 1 means the odds are the same whatever the value of the predictor.






JASP reports an Estimate of 0.693 for a predictor Sex (Female). What is the odds ratio, and what does it mean?

0.693: women’s odds are about 31% lower than men’s
2.0: women’s odds are twice men’s
1.693: women are 69% more likely than men to be in the outcome category
You cannot tell without the p-value







TipAnswer





b. The odds ratio is e0.693 ≈ 2.0, so women’s odds are about twice men’s. Option c confuses odds with probability (and uses the wrong conversion). JASP shows the Odds Ratio column by default, so you rarely need to do this by hand.






In the BSA 2010 model, Sex (Female) has an odds ratio of 0.646. Which statement is correct?

Women are 35% less likely than men to say most people can be trusted
Among people of the same age, women’s odds of trusting are about 35% lower than men’s
The probability that a woman trusts most people is 0.646
Being a woman causes lower trust







TipAnswer





b. (0.646 − 1) × 100 = −35%, and this is a change in odds, adjusted for age. Statement a describes probabilities, which differ by about 11 percentage points (see Question 9). Statement d makes a causal claim that survey data alone cannot support.






When you first fit the BSA 2010 model, JASP notes that “Can’t be too careful in dealing with people” has been coded as class 1. What does the model describe?

The probability of trusting most people
The probability of not trusting most people
Nothing: JASP fixes the coding automatically
The mean of SocTrust







TipAnswer





b. Logistic regression models the probability of the category coded 1, and JASP codes the second category as 1. All coefficients would flip sign. Reverse the label order (or recode) so that 1 = “Most people can be trusted”.






You need to dichotomise a 1-5 trust scale, and the most common answer is the unlabelled middle value, 3. What is the best practice?

Always group the middle value with the higher values
Try both cut-points and report the one with the smaller p-value
Choose the cut on conceptual grounds before seeing the results, report it, and check whether a reasonable alternative changes the conclusions
Drop everyone who answered 3







TipAnswer





c. In the BSA 2010 self-completion question, the conclusions about age and sex flip depending on where the 3s go (Worksheet 4, Exercise 4.1.1). Choosing the cut by its p-value (b) is a form of p-hacking; dropping a quarter of the sample (d) throws away data and changes who you are studying.






The BSA 2010 model with age and sex has a Nagelkerke R² of 0.019. Which reading is right?

Age and sex together account for only a very small share of the variation in trust
The model explains 19% of the variation in trust
The coefficients for age and sex are not statistically significant
The model has been fitted incorrectly







TipAnswer





a. Pseudo-R² measures like Nagelkerke’s are rough guides, but 0.019 is very small. A small R² is common for attitudes and does not mean the coefficients are wrong or non-significant: the sex coefficient has p < .001.






The model predicts that a 20-year-old man has a 47% probability of saying most people can be trusted, and a 20-year-old woman 36%. How big is the sex difference in probability terms?

35%
About 11 percentage points
0.646
1.98







TipAnswer





b. 47% − 36% ≈ 11 percentage points, and the gap is similar at every age. This is the clearest way to tell a general reader how big the difference is. The 35% (a) and 0.646 (c) describe odds, not probabilities.






If you fit a linear regression to the 0/1 SocTrust outcome with age and sex, the coefficient for Sex (Female) is −0.108. What does it mean?

Women are about 10.8 percentage points less likely than men of the same age to say most people can be trusted
Women’s odds of trusting are 10.8% lower
The log-odds of trusting are 0.108 lower for women
Women are 0.108 times as likely to trust







TipAnswer





a. With a 0/1 outcome, a linear regression coefficient is a difference in probability. Here it almost exactly matches the logistic model’s predictions, because all the predicted probabilities sit between 35% and 60%, where the logistic curve is close to a straight line.

Trust reduces inequality (trusting societies support redistribution)
Something else, such as history or institutions, drives both
None of them







TipAnswer





d. A correlation is compatible with all three stories. To weigh them we need theory, other variables (Week 3: multiple regression lets us adjust for some third factors) and ideally data over time.
